I HAVE been trying (says Josh Billings) for the past forty years to find out at what time of life a man is most foolish, and when I find out I'll let you know. WIGGINS, the weather prophet, seems to have .gone into the coal business. He predicts a winter that will bury last year's record under ten feet of snow.

THE Vise man forseeth the evil and prepareth into himself a cyclone pit. Even if the tornado fails to arrive the pit will come in handy during family disturbances. "BRIDGET, did you hear the door bell?" "Yes'm," "Why don't you go to the door then." "Sure. an' it's nobody to see me. I'm not expectiu' callers CUSTOM compels an Icelander in his native island to kiss every woinan he meets. It must make an Icelander mad to discover his wife bearing down on him from the opposite side of the way.

It's that .thin he's getting that when he dies not a body there'll be to wake, at all, at all."
THE best way to get along with people who are "set up with pride" is to upset their pride, and them, too.

"YOUNG MAN," said a cross old lady on a street ear, "terbacker-smoking make me sick." It used to make me sick, too, ma'am,' replied the young man, lighting a fresh cigar; "but there you'll get used to it after a while." •

ONCE, whilst Lamb was waiting in the Highgate stage, a woman came to the door and inquired in a stern voice, "Are you quite full inside ?" " 'Yes, ma'am," said Charles, in meek reply, "quite; that plateful of Mrs. Gillman's pudding has quite filled as."

"Din you hear about the burglar who was arrested this morning ?" " No ! What for ?" "For breaking into song." "Is that so I" "Yes. He'd got through, two bars, when some one hit him with a stave." Funeral piiivate. "Tummy, is your sister Clarinda in?" " Mebby she is and mebby she ain't. What's your name r ." Why do you ask ?", " Waal, ye see, she said if -Mr. Tompkins called she'd be in, but if old Cruik- shank came she'd be out. Which be you ?" Mr. •Cruikshank departed. A LADY in Edinburgh, the mother of a large family of interesting children, has never struck one a blow in anger. When a child does wrong .she keeps a bottle of castor oil and rhubarb on the mantle and at once forces the culprit to take a dose a the mixture.

JOHN REED, the gaslighter uf the Walnut Street Theatre, Philadelphia, concluded his Will with this strange wish :—" My head to be separated from my body, duly macerated and prepared, then to be employed to represent the skull of Yorick in the play of Hamlet.' "—Cassell's Magazine. AN old miser kept a tame jackdaw that used to steal pieces of money and hide them in a hole. The cat observed this, and asked why he would hoard up those round_shining.things.that he could make

no use of. "Why," said the jackdaw, "my master has a whole chestfall, and makes no more use of -them than I." A YOUNG LADY who affected a disinclination -towards matrimony, wrote on a pane of glass some verses expressive 'of her determination never to enter .into the holy state. A gentleman, who doubted the: _ lady's resolve, wrote underneath "The fair, whose vows these scratchy buss betoken, Wrote thorn on glass—she knew it would be broken t"' A 'LEADING minister of New York was preaching from the text—" Thou are weighed to the balance :and:found wanting." He was very much annoyed. by people leaving the church during the sermon, and finally stopped and said "That's right, brethren—as fast as you are weighed pass out I" The exodus -Stopped. PATCHOULY is a perfume derived from an East Indian plant of the Labiatce family, not very far iremoved from our common mint. It is used by the East Indians to give the peculiar odour of Indian shawls. Since this has been discovered, shawls made in England are perfumed with patchouly, and then palmed off on an innocent public as "genuine Cashmere shawls." _

IT is reported in an American electrical joumal that many dead centipedes have been observed or, the ground in the vicinity of electric lights. These animals are believed to thrive in dark place ,34 but whether it is the rays of light, or electricity escap- ing from the wires, which kills them, has nut yet been ascertained. "How are you to-day, my dear?" asked the -High School girl of her friend aa nhey met. this morning. "Oh. I feel wider the weather to-day, ' Mildred," was the reply, "Had you not better say subordinated to meteorological conditions of the atmosphere,' instead cf under the weather ? gently corrected Mildred. "This chilly weather makes me think of my poor, dead husband," said a widow, as she sat down beside a lady close to the fire. "He was always so cold, poor man, and he need to wonder if he ever would get warmed through. He was so miserable when he was cold, poor man, but it is a great coni- . fort to me to feel that he is a happy man now." "So, Mr. Witness, you swear that at the time this theft was committed on the south side you saw the prisoner on the north side." "Yes, sir." "Was he going toward the south side or was lie coming from that direction." "I can't answer that now." "Why not 7" "Because the prisoner's lawyer forgot to tell me which way north is."

"WAS it raining very hard when you came in?" asked Bobby of 'Featherly, who was making an evening call. " Raining 2 " said Featherly. "Cer- tainly not. The stars were out." " It's funny," continued Bobby, thoughtfully. "Pa had a gentle- man here to dinner to-night, and I heard ma say 'se you came up the steps; that it never rains but it Tours." "SYMPATHISING FRIEND—" Is it true, my dear Mrs. Brown, that you husband committed suicide 2 " Mrs. Brown (recently beraaved)—" I am afraid it is." Sympathising friend—" What in the world in- duced him to commit suoli a rash and desperate a.ot " "Mrs. Brown—" I haven't the faintest idea. I uever knew John to do such a thing before."

The frst wife knocked all the romance out of me; the second taught me humility." "And your present wife ? " "Made a philosopher out of me. I can bear other people's troubles with a great deal of Eelf-complacency." "WHEN I want my children to mind," said Mrs. "I never stopped to explain the reasons to them. I just put my foot down, and that's the end of "Oh, well," responded Twitters, absent- mindedly, "that covers the ground completely, of course; there's no need for explanation." For a few moments it was a mere toss-up whether Twit- te.rs might not be ignominiously spanked. "WHAT good does preachin' do, anyhow?" was a question which astounded Bobby's mother at Sun- day dinner. "It does a deal of good, my little boy," she replied. "It makes people better and happier in every way. "It doesn't affect pa in that way," continued Bobby. "When we went to church this morning pa was feeling first-rate, but when we got home and found that dinner was half an hour late you wouldn't think preachin' made people better or happier if you'd see him."

It Was an actor on Saturday who said, as he read the names on the p:rogram of the performance of "School," at the Garrick Theatre," School ' ; Irving jun., Hare, jun. ; why, it must be the Infant School."

It is no news that Sir Arthur Sullivan is writing a new comic opera, the libretto of which is the work of a writer whose name is kept a secret. 4 The name of the writer of the libretto will come as a surprise to most people. It is Mr. W.S. Gilbert: Sir Arthur has just returned from Contrexeville, with his health much improved by the cure he has been following.

Professor Windscheid, of Leipzig, one of the most eminent jurists now living has gone over to the Protestant Church out of indignation, as is said, a*,./ the exhibition of the Holy Coat at Tr6ves. This converAon, a Berlin Correspondent says, causP,s all the more sensation as profeegOr Windschied belongs to an old Rhenish Catholic family,, and enjoys the highest esteem among men of science. •

Locusts have been doing great havoc in the su- burbs of Yangchow, in China, but strange to say, so far they had only devoured the green reeds and leaves of trees, leaving all the crops untouched. The Chinese farmers consider this a special inter- vention of Providence, and at the last dates were subscribing to get up a theatrical performance for three days to express their gratitude.

Sir Richard Moon, Bart., ex-chairman of the Lon- don and North-Western Railway; was seventy-even on Tuesday. Sir Richard, who is' a Jubilee baronet, has his seat at Copsewood Grange, near Coventry, where he spends a very quiet life, taking nowt in local affairs. Miss Moon, his daughter, is, however, occasionally active in Primrose League work. Copsewood. a small tate, adjoins/ the War wick- shire estate of the Earl of Craven. •

Lord and Lady Harris, who are both devoted to cricket, have early begun to make a little cricketer of the baby heir. At the chilaren's fancy dress ball recently given by Mrs. Pottinger at Poona, Lord and Lady Harris were accompanied by the nurse carrying in her arms the Hon. George Vincent Harris, whose tiny form was iarrayed in the most correct of cricket suits to personate a "Kent cricketer."

The story of Mrs. Besant having seen letters written by the prophetess Blavatsky since her de- cease reminds one of the anecdote of Lady Mary Topham, the well-known sister of the late Duke of Portland. and Samuel "Warren, the nuthor of "Ten Thousand a Year." "These eyes have seen the hand- writing 'cif the dead; and seeing is believing, Mr. Warren," exclaimed, Lady Mary. "Yes," replied Warren, "and believing is seeing:*

By Monday's Australian mail we learn from the "Melbourne Herald" that "in Cie event of the .world-renowned preacher, the Revr. C. IL Spurgeon, recoverirg sufficiently to be able to nsume work, it is the intention of the leading Baptists of Victoria to invite the rev, gentleman to pay a visit to the colony. They believe the trip vvill recuperate his strength and energy, and at the same time lead to a great religious revival in Australia.

Lord and Lady Aberdeen are at preserat staying on the farm which Lord Aberdeen purchased last year to the east of Vancouver. It .is a pretty little pro- perty of under a hundred acres, a typical British Columbian settlers" lot." The Earl and his wife have both thoroughly relished their colonial holiday trip. Yext month they will visit Chicago. While there Lady Aberdeen intends to use all Iter influ- ence with the executive of the World 'A- Fair in favor of the Irish Industrial Association.

A Social Questions Committee, formed itreonnec- tion wit h.the Congregational Union, to "give infor- maticn, advice, and other assistance in fuctherance of upward social movements," has nominated Mr. Albert Speer as their Chairman and the Rey. C. Fleming Williams as their Secretary. In Russia. society at large, even in' the capitals has been so constantly deprived of all initiative that it is utterly powerless to organise at a moment like the present effective relief, whatever individual charity roay achieve. Colonel,' MacGregor, whose Wife has just met her terrible death in the Engadine, has held his post of Assistant-Adjutant General at the Horse Guards for about a vwelvemonth. A tall handsome man' rather ' above middle age, with a marked military hearing, he nossesses that rare appendage to a soldier's" qualifications—business tat. For an offitial in the Civil Service be is a tremendous worker, executing in fact„many of the eilerationS in the army's equip- ment attd promotion,. for which the Duke of Cam- bridge and Sir Redvers Buller get most Othe credit. Besides his official tinties, he is keenly interested in evangelistic work, and his sympathies in this direction, it is said, are as publicly outspoken as they are privately benevolent. He had only been back from his annixtl leave ten days when a telegrams on Friday morning recalled him to Switzerland.

Miss Mabel Besant, who has just reached the naa of twenty-one, is an exceedingly pretty girl, with short black curly hair and a round fan, somewlfat like her mother's at the time the old portraits we published. UnfortunatelY;bowever. she does- it possess Mrs. Annie Besant's physical strength-, and she spent last winter in the South of France in opder to regain her health. She is now a great trioycle rider and.cigarette smoker: but does not show 7inch inclination to become a TheosophiSt. Time will, perhaps, remedy this defect, her friends say,_ as— unfortunately—it will remove the girlish Light- heartedness for which she is noted. She is seen .at her best when teaching or playing with,- children, and therefore the occupation of a daily governess which she has chosen for hersalf is. paculiarly appropriate to her. ,

Her speechfin response to the toast of he7health was brief and modest. One was perforce reminded of Mrs. Besant's account of her maiden speech, de- iireTed to a solitary audience. lit• was whils living with her husband at Sibsey that, one day, havincz entered the church to practise en the organ, and locked the door, she mounted the pulpit, and then and there delivered her first Mauro. "I shall never forget," she has said, "the feeling of power and de- light which came upon me as iny voice rolled do-on. the aisles, and the passion in me broke into bid:. anced sentences, and never paused for rhythmical expression; while I felt that all I wanted was to see the church full of upturned' faces, insteud of the emptiness of the silent pews." But that soli- tary lecture was the maiden speech of the,first lady orator of our time.

A correspondent in the "Daily Chronicle " °as' attention to the atrocious cruelty inflicted on the deer in Windsor-park by the Queen's staghounds. The pack of staghounds are kept up at the public expense, and serve no other purpose thanto torture the deer. The sport carried on belongs to the order of antiquated barbarisms which flourished in the days when there was no S.P.C.A., of which the Queen is patron. The deer .are first driven into paddocks, and their antlers are sawn off. When a meet takes place, the animals are conveyed .in a covered cart and liberated amongst a croWd of excited people. The hounds are then set upon them. The deer are compelled to run ; they tear themselves on barbed wire, take shelter in sheds d houses, and are frequently worried by the ahnounds. nd this is done in the Queen's name.

The news of Sir James Fergusson's appointment came as a surprise to the Post Office officials, who seem to have made up their minds that Mr. Jack- son would succeed 3.1 r. Raikes. But it is univers- ally acknowledged in the department that Lord Salisbury has made .an excellent selection, as Sir James has a reputation at the Foreign Office, for tact,bard work, and discretion. The Theosophist craze has at length gone the way of all ocher crazes, and has become an intoler- able nuisance. The disciples of the Mahatmas had great hopes that Mrs. Besant's conversion would be followed by that of many other friends and admirers. All went well at first, but to the dismay of the Theosophists Mr. Stuart Cumberland's ,chal- lenge was accepted by &certain Colonel Desnfond; who, after professing him Self to'put the matter to the test and to risk .El,OOO on the result, backed out of it on the ground that he had received orders from Thibet not to gratify the vulgar curiosity of sceptics. The Theosophists now assert that the letter purporting to come from Colonel Desmond was a hoax, and that the gallant colonel is a myth. However that may be, the refusal to accept Mr. Stuart Cumberland's offer. has, immensely damaged the Theosophists' cause, as it is clear that if the Mahatmas possessed the remarkable powers attri- buted tci them nothing would be easier than for them to perform miracles which would convert Professor Huxley, Mr. Labouchere, and other un- believers in Theosophy.

IChicago is pre-eminently a theatre city, and its people support no less than 26, big and little, as well as numerous other entertainments. Sunday labour is very prevalent. The cable cars run as on week days, and all sorts of occupations are carried on. Shops are open, , and street 'vendors continue their trade without a break. Fainters, paper- bangers, decorators, hairdressers?' and the like know no Sunday rest. Bricklayers and builders have no respite on the first day of the week, and all the railway excursions appear to be arranged for that day. Irree tickets are scattered broad-cast for Sunday tripe to some newly" boomed" city to enable people to select .lots. Whilst I was in the city one of these parties nearly 'Came to grief. They went out on a house hunting expedition some six or seven miles from the city, when some of the juveniles fired the dry graes, and the party had to flee for their lives. In a certain portion of the city no respectable person—male or fernale—is to be found. To such a pitch has- ;he wickedness of the city arrived that the pastor of the church I attended twice publicly alluded to end deplored it.

In addition to their spacious streets, American cities are well provided with breathing places. Public squares, gardens, and parks are as frequently met with as in continental cities. To this national characteristic, the City of Destiny is no exception. It has eight extensive and well-kept parks in various parts of the city. The three largest border on or are in close proiximity to the Lake, which gives to them an additional charm. On the north is Lincoln Park, a well wooded and beamtiful retreat of 295 acres. At the entranceiS a large and famousmonu- ment to America's first murdered, President, and in the grounds is a small Zoological garden, which is a great source of attraction to visitors. A small lion, a tiger, a few unhappy-looking birds, arid some small monkeys are shelteved in a pavilion,, and out- side are bearpits, a small herd of buffaloes, and a melancholy elephant tetlrared by its fore l'eg to a stake driven in the ground,and Which cuts a fpotesque but distressing figure as he- tries- tei get bin trunk ,within reach of the contributions of visitors. It Lwas Sunday when I visited the park, and' the .grounds swarmed with peoplein brilliant auramer attire. Amongst them were' whole families, ap- Lparently cut for the day. Judged by the English standard Chicago is un- donbtedly a wicked city. Just now the city has got for Mayor a man who has insisted upon the Sunday closing of the saloons, but all the restaurants have open doors on the Sabbath. Mingo Pete stood high in his "profession." His fellow-criminals looked up to him wi something like adoration, and they obeyed him assmaquestion- ingly as the soldier: obeys a beloved uomma.nder. Men. the officers offthe law, whose wits had been putt to the severest test to bailie him, spoke of his exploits with something like admiration. He was a strange combination of ignorance and cunning, of brutality and courage. He might have been born without any moral capacity so+fax as any vestige of principle remained to him at the age of forty. To deceive Allen Gilbert, who at heart was all guileless as a child, was not indeed a 'wonderful exploit; yet he was so much Mingo's superior in intelligence that the outlaw felt as prDed of his sacoess as if he hadplundered a bank single- Landed. _ .
At Pine Place, where 'Mingo met up with Allen after both were free,. ,he found Minnie, 'aye unfor- tunate woman whom he called his wife.

'What do you mean?" he asked,,threateningly. " I'm not blind,'" she replied. "No, but you 're a fool." "I didn't ask you to tell ma what you was doing. Did you,expect me to press my- lips and listen in silence Z.: Maybe I 'T..7.e been silent too long, but I 'll say this-for last, and I:mean it:" She took a backward step, clasped her hands above the shawl, and added, with a tremor of the thin nos- , trils and a contraction of the eyelids that gave her ' face a dangerous expression: "If you hurt him, ' you hurt he and while I've got a heart, and a memory, and a tongue, aint agoing to stand by like a dummy and See that done.' "What 1 Are you 'posin' me again? Goin' to kick and blow, are you.?" He strode towards her with up-li4ted hand, and shouting a vile name, he added: "I've allus 'spected you was glad when; I was sent up before., Do you want to get rid ck me again, eh 7 " She made no effort to avoid the threatened blw, made no movement, except to insert her right b.,and inside her shawl; but an awful light took, the place of the hunted look in her eyes, and her thin, colourless lips were drawn back from hez- even, white teeth.

In a voice thrilling in its intensity, thorgh sunk almost to a whisper, Minnie said: "You swore, Pete, you'd never strike:me agab, and when last you trampled me under your feet, and I got up crushed and bleeding, I took an oath that, if you ever tried that thing again, you or me would die., Before you strike, ask yourself which it is to be,"

- Flolence was quite as humane and generous as her brother; but though her sex may be charged with impulse in their estimates of men, they have an intuitive perception of motives that no- amount of experience will give- to man. "I know you are actin.. for the best, dear brother," she said; "but I should not give this man my. confldense until he has proved himself worthy of it, after a thorough trial. "Well, Flcsrie, I can't be half-hearted,"' was Allen's reply, "If. he tLinks I suspect him, he will fly ofi. • If I had never suffered myself —if I had neves.known what it what it was tebe under the harrow of a cruel fate—l might demand 'fruit meet for .sepentance,' but as it is, God help— ing me, I shall try to help him without question." At length a place was secured for Mingo, as night- watchman fora large jewellery establishment near Madison Square; and he entered on his duties with a vigour and intelligence which his employers be- lieved argued well for the future. Meanwhile, the world went better and better with Allen. He would have left the tenement for more desirable quartets, had it no4J, been for the intense interest of himself and Flcrenee in their less favoured neighbours. The night school progressed.finely, and the sew- ing women and sewing men, whe constituted the bulk of the tenants, took more interest in their rooms, and on the stairs and halls- leading to them, and, se improved the place so much, that the land- lord,, who had not;-:visited the building for years, sericusly discussed'with his agent the advisability of raising the rent. Irene Lefferts's interest in the sehool, and in the • brother and sister who had organised it, increased from day to day, until at last the elevation- of the poor became the ruling object of her life. In this good work her father supported her nobly, and if be noticed thogrowing intimacy between his daughter and Allen Gilbert, as he-surely must have done;, he had too m-ach faith in hone to ask for an explanation before sitewas ready to volunteer her confidence. Nothing is more useful to a politician than the ability to ignore a troublesome opponent's exist— ence. Beaconsfield, as everybody. knows, had Such alaculty. .11e possessed a sort of detached lever arrangement, whereby., he shut out of sight and hearing that which he did not wish to see and hear. Would that vre.sitcould clothe same!' This iron self-control is, however,. sotare that only One member of Parliament is endowed with it, and that fortunate one is Lord Hartington. In stormy days the badgers or the Irish,party.made many attemPts to." draw " him; but by degrees they realised that their efforts were futile, and for some years now .they have let him alone. The characteristic atti- tude, of the noble marqness• when in the House of Commons is well known. lie site with outstretched. legs, hands in pockets, andliat tilted over•eyesi looking the personificatiOn of indifference. The Prince. of Wales Can: boast of a wonderful memory for names and facies,,as, indeed, can nearly all the members af our Royal. family ;, and &highly -valuable attribute it is. Mr. Gladstone has several .very rare endowments, not the least remafable of ' which is his doable conSdousuess. When he likes ,he can become absorbed in.one thing to ele exclu- ' sion of everything else;„lwith equal facility he can :direct his thoughts into two entirely different ! Channels. Ducringthe time he was last inAffice the.. ex-Premier attended to a great deal of his enorm- otis Correspondence white seated on ths Treasury Bench. Bent over his writing pad. he seemed en- grossed wits his letter& sad. post-cards, as his hand.. travelled rapidly acrossthe paper. Butoif anybody misquoted him, ormede a statement not in accord with fe.cts,,Mr. Gladstone shook his leonine head,. or, springing to his feet, hurled back Alt, retort, and then resumed his seat and went on 77(,..ting. How.- many men could dothis ? Before turning from mental to yhysical endow-. meats of the" freak" order, we reny mention the throat of Mr. Fred Leslie, the well-known actor.. According to an, eminent specialist„- that organ is. uniquely adapted for mimicry. 14, differs as much from ordinary throats as does, say„Patti's or Pori's.. Hence the successful imitations,of this comedian, are due not to, study and practice, but to natural: gifta• Of the men who prove natures.fertility in variety. we must content ourselves with only two orthree ergimples. lissrd Wemyss is said to have the power of moving his ears at will. 'More oddly endowed is T4ord Ducie,, whose eyes are of distinctly different colours ;one is black and piecing; the other bright -and blue. His lordship sometimes takes.amusing iadvantages of this peculiarity, which by-the-bye, has been handed down front generatioiato genera- tion in his family. When introduced to kgenthaman he holds his eyeglass so that only one. eye can be seen. At the next glance- which the new acquain- tenanee takes, Lord Dude turns on him the other optic. The result, say those who have seen this little trick, is very funny, and one can readily im- agine that it is.—Calvales Saturday *journal,

div.head: REVISION COURTS.
div.p: THE REVISION COURTS.

NEWTON DIVISION. EtLuso& Mr. J. T.. Foard c)ntinued his revision of the lists of voters for the Newton Parliamentary Division on Thurs- day week, when he held a court at the National Schools, Billings. Mr. S. J. Harrison, registration agent for the Darwen division, and Mr. W. Ripley appeared for the Liberals, and Mr. W. H. Brook, solicitor, and Mr. W. Holbrook, agent for the Conservatives. A PRIEST'S TOTS. The Liberals had issued an objection to the, voteidf the Rev. rather Austin Powell, of Birchley Catholic Chapel, on the ground that his qtalifying property was not 'free- hold, and Father Powell appeared to sustain his vote. Restated, in answer to questions, that he was thesowner of 'freehold houses and land connected with Birchley Chapel, and added that he had been on the list of voters and had voted for the last 19 years.—Mr. 'Earrison expressed the opinion that the vote was quite in order, and attributed the issuing of the notice of objection to an error on the part•of his party.—Mr. Brook remarked :that Father Powell had been objected to by the party 'which he had supnorted.—The Barrister &lowed the `vote to remain on the register, and considered the objec- tion to be of a frivolous character.—Father'Powell asked if he was to be allowed any expenses for his attendance. —The Barrister remarked that he was entitled to eapenses, but be would lave the amount to the generosity of the Liberal party.—Mr. 'Harrison then handed a sum .of money to Father tPowell, but the amount did not-transpire.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
On Friday, Mr. Foard held a sitting at the County Court, St. Helens, Messrs. Brook and t olbrook appear- ing for the Conservatives, and Messrs.'W. Ripley and J. Bain for the Liberals.

div.head: NO NOTICE.
div.p: NO NOTICE.

The Liberals objected to the vote of 'John Sephton, of Ormskirk-road, Rainford, and on the revising barrister asking for the copy of the notice <if objection. Mr. Rip-, ley said he had not brqught it. The Barrister: Then what is the-objection ? Mr. Ripley: I don't know, your Honour. I don't remember. The Barrister (to Mr. Brook) : Do you know what the objection is? Mr. Brook: No, sir; I have not seen it. The Barrister: The name is printed on the Bit of objections. and I will deal with it. In reply to questions, the claimant stated that during the past year he had removed from one house to asaother, and he had not claimed for successive occupa- tion.--His Honour thereupon disallowed the vote.

THE VALI7E OF A 'RENT BOOK. The Conservatives objected to the vote of a man named Jones, of Ormskirk-road, Rainford, who, in ans- wer to the barrister, said he had left his rent book at home.—Vhe Barrister: Why have you not brought it? Jones I did not think it would be ziecessary.—The Barrister: But you have to prove your claim, and the rent book would be the best evidence.—Jones : I have lived in the house for two years.—The Barrister: %But because you say so we are not obliged to accept it. We want proof. If every man who came up here to claim a vote had only to have his word accepted to get the vote we should have the register filled by a lot of people who had no right to be on.—The vote was ultimately allowed.

CONTRADICTORY'STATEMENTS. Thomas Sparks, of Harding's-row, Rai nford," a ppeared te sustain his vote, which was objected to by the Con- servatives. In this case Sparks had not brought his rent book, and Mr. Brook asked for the vote to be struck off on the ground that the occupancy during the qualifying period could not be proved. Their objection was that the Lean had moved from one house to another during the twelve months.—Sparks said that that was not the case, and produced a note from the Rainford Coal Company, the owners of the property, dated the 14th September, as follows :—" This is to certify that Thomas Sparks nas occupied one of the company's cottages at Harding's- row, since May, 1885." He. added that he had , lived in his present house over 15 months without any removal. —Mr. Brook remarked that-the note from the owners did not specify any particular house and that the note wasnot evidence.—Mr. J. Ellison, a worker for the Con- servative party, stated that in the first week of July last he visited the property and was informed that Sparks had removed from No. 34 to No. 35 during the qualifying period.—Sparks then took the oath, and said that he had not moved during a period of 15 months, and the Barrister allowed the vote. Sparks-: Can I have my expenses for coming here ? The Barrister: You have given us a great deal of trouble which you might have saved yourself by bringing or sending the rent book. No; I cannot assist you in any way.

div.head: CONCLUSION AND THANKS,
div.p: CONCLUSION AND THANKS,

This,concluded the revision of the Newton Division lists, and W. El. Brook, on behalf of all who had attended the proceedings, expressed their thanks to the revising barrister for the consideration and patience he had ex- tended towards them during the inquiries. He was happy to say that there had not been a word of unplea- santness during the whole course of the revision and he thought the only indication of anything of the kind that they had had was on one occasion when the barrister stated that if they did insist on taking him back tcpcases he had already settled he should set his face against it. He again begged to thank his Honour for his kindness and help.—Mr. Ripley, on behalf of-the Liberal party, cor- dially supported the observations of Mr. Brook.—The Barrister: lam very much obliged to you for your as- sistance, and I am glad that, with one exception—Rain- ford—the overseers have done their work exceedingly well, and better, in some respects, than they have done before. lam glad to see your improvement, because the work goes on much more smoothly and easier. I should like to see the Rainford lists numbered as far as they can be, and I should have spoken to the overseer about it, but he has not been present. I thank you all for your attendance and courtesy.

div.head: ST. HELENS. SATURDAY.
div.p: ST. HELENS. SATURDAY.

The revision of the lists of voters for the borough of St. Helens was resumed before Mr. J. T. Foard, revising barrister, at the Town Hall, on Saturday forenoon. Mr. J. P. Mearna, solicitor, and Mr. J. Bain, agent, appea red forithe Liberals, and Messrs. J. 0. Swift, solicitor, and W. Lamb, agent, for the Conservatives. AN ABUSE OF THE FRANCHISE. Henry Broadhead claimed a lodger vote at his father 's house and shop, Church-st. He stated that he paid 6s. 6d. for the use of the rooms he occupied, and his board was separate. He had paid the 63. 6d. per week for nine years, and had been on the register before. The Barrister remarked that there was no evidence of an absolute tenancy, and it looked much like an arrange- ment to obtain a vote. He should have liked some in- dependent evidence.—Mr. Mearns ; This gentleman, if he liked, could take a separate house, but he prefers to live with his parents.—The Barrister decided to allow the vote, but he said it seemed an abuse of the fran- chise.

THE WRONG RENT BOOS. Mrs. Bilmorey, of Railway-street, appeared to support the claim of her husband, Patrick, to a vote. The claim was successive occupation of houses on Canal-bank and Railway-st. The Conservatives objected on the ground that the claimant had resided in Atlas-street, nut this was denied by Mrs. Bilmorey. She produced four rent books, one cf which was marked "9, Atlas-st." On this being pointed out to her, she said she had brought the wrong book. She could not explain why "9, Atlas-street," was written in the book. She had never lived in Atlas-street.—Mr. Mearns contended that the words 9, Atlas-street," were written in error for "9, Canal-bank." After some diseussion the Barrister remarked that he could only assume an error .had been made by some clerk, and he should have liked a better explanation. He would, however, allow the vote.

THE PUBLIC-HOUSE MANAGERSHIP QUESTION. The Liberals objected to the vote of Joseph Cook, of the Ramford Hotel, on the ground that he was not the tenant of the hotel, but the manager for a brewery com- pany. He stated that he had @coupled the house for 18 months. Mr. Bain: Are you not the manager for Messrs. Walker and Co.? Mr. Cook: Yes, the responsible manager.—The Barrister: Then you will be struck off the municipal list and be allowed the parliamentary vote only.—Mr. Cook: All the managers in St. Helens are on the list.—The Barrister: Yes; all the managers in such cases, managing for brewing firms, get parliamentary votes but not municipal votes.

div.head: EXPENSIVE TO THE LIBERALS.
div.p: EXPENSIVE TO THE LIBERALS.

The Liberals had issued objections to eight or nine voters OR the list for Newton-road, on the ground that their residence was wrongly described. The eoutention was that the correct description was liavanna-road. After some discussionit Appeared that the correct name was Newton:road, and all,the votes were allowed. The sum of about £2 was paid out. in expenses by the Liberal agent.

LIVELY PASSAGE OF ARMS. The vote of Mr. William Harvey,?f the Sutton Brewery, was objected to by the Conservatives on the ground *Of wrong description of qualifying property. He sustained his vote, and asked for expenses.—The Barrister: Let me see, brewing is a very bad business uow.—Mr. Mearns : Very good, I should say, at present..—The Barrister: What do you claim P—Mr. Harvey I should like the full amount you can allow me .—Mr. Swift: Of course he loses nothing.—Mr. Harvey: My time.—Mr. Mearns : The question is, how many guineas de you claim 2—Mr. Harvey : Oh,l don't want to rob the people. —Mr. Mearns :* There is no robbing.—The Barrister : Well, I will allow you 53.—Mr: Harvey (astonished) : Five shillings! 'Why, I had to COME three times about the vote.—Mr. Mearns : And your HOGOUr allowed a small rope manufacturer, who had no right to be on the list, 10s. 61. for being here half-an-hour. ' (To Mr. Harvey) : Open your mouth.—The Barrister: No, no. Mr. ' Harvey has lost very little time as far as

I can see. He has not been here more thanhalf-an-hour. —Mr. Harvey : It is the best part of the day.—Mr. Mearns : And his place of business is three miles away. —The Barrister: That is another matter, and I will allow him 7s. 6d.—Mr. Swift : I do think Mr. Mearns ought to have some regard for decency. He says behind Mr. Glover's back what he dare not say to his face, and A do protest against it.—Mr. Mearns: Yes, I dare say it.— "The Barrister said that he knew the case, and it appeared that the voter had always gone by the name of Glover; that he was known as Glover ; and he thought it was not proper to raise the paint again.—Mr. Svvitt said he was always known as Mr. Glover, and was never tailed by any other name. He again alluded to Mr. Mearns's con- duct as being "positively indecent.'—The Barrister remarked that he thought Mr. Mearns had alluded to the case in rather strong terms.—Mr. Mearns drew the attention of his Honour to the fact that he had not mentioned any narre.—Mr. Swift: You referred to the case in such terms that everybody knows to whom you referred.—The suliect then dropped.

THE POLICE FRANCHISE. James Winnard, a member of the borotgh police force, claimed a vote for successive occupation of houses, a, Clyde-st.' and 247, Burton-head-road.—Mr. Mearns stated that he was a police officer, and there was no ob- jection.—The 33arrister remarked,that as a police officer., he wouldonly be on the parliamentary list.—Mr. Mearna said he thought they had the question discussed last year.—Mr. 'Swift said he thought they were allowed on all the lists last year.—The Barrister : They may have been printed so,but properly they cannot be on the muni- cipal list. They cannot vote as burgesses except under: a severe renalty.—Mr.Swift said'he thought police officers were allowed to remain on theregister so that in case they left the' force they would notibe debarred from votirrg.— The Barrister pointed out. thelt:llaron Pollock had deoided a case upon that point;' and his decision he (Mr. Fooard) had adopted, and it was generally adopted by other re- visers. Baron Pollock said 'the woids were absolutely specific, and they deprived revising barristers of the power to leave them on thellist. That was theiffect of thedecision.—Mr. Mearns,..: Then it was rather unfor- tunate that I mentioned he was a palice officer. (Laugh- terl)—The Barrister: Yes, it would have been better as the name stood.—Censtable 'Winnard's 'name was then struck off the municipal list, and he was allowei a parliamentary vote. The Court afterwards adjourned until Menday. MONDAY.

The revision of the lists of voters for the .b6iough was ,continned at the Town Hall, on Monday, before Mr. J. :Foard. Mr. J. 0. Swift (solicitor) and Mr. W. Lamb (agent) appeared for the Conservatives and Mr. W. Bain (agent) for the Liberals. The business consisted of the reading over of the lists for the various wards.

UN-NUMBERED HDUSEIII. Whilst the lists for 'West Sutton were under Considera- tion, Mr. Kitchen (assistant overseer) pointed, out that in Royal-street, Thatto Heath, and in other streets of the town the houses were not numbered, and in some cases the numbers given to him were only supposed numbers. Under those circumstances there was no definite way of describing qualifying property.—His Honour said that, unnumbered houses'were contrary. to the Public Health Act.—Mr. Kitchen: As a matter of fact they are in courts and yards, and there are no numbers.—The Barrister asked if the Corporation were the rural sanitary authority ?—Mr. Kitchen : They are, sir.—Mr.Lea (chief clerk) : But most of their powers are under a !ocal Act. Mr. Kitchen: Mr. Jeeves (town clerk) promised last year that he would have them correctly numbered.— The Barrister said he did not how the position of the Corporation was affeeted by their local Act, but he thought it desirable that some attention should be given to the matter.—Mr. Kitchen repeated that he had not inserted the numbers of the houses in the list as the houses were not numbered, and supposed numbers sup- plied to him made his list a miserable one.—His Honour said he would get over the difficulty this time by describ- ing them as Back Royal-st., &c.

div.head: TRH B-ARRISTER'S POWERS.
div.p: TRH B-ARRISTER'S POWERS.

The Barrister drew attention to a case before him on Saturday week, when he decided to strike off a name en the register and insert that of another claimant for the same house. At the time Mr. Swift asked if his Honour could strike the name off without notice to the individual, and the Barrister replied that he had the power to do so. Yesterday the Barrister remarked that wherever a mis- take appeared to have been made in the lists he had the power to correct it. It seemed to him that in the case in question there was a clear mistake,and sole held that whether there was an objection or not he was bound to correct it. The words of the Act were clear--" He shall correct any mistake which has been proved to be made." He should alwaTs consider where there were two names for the same qualifying house that there was some mis- take,and his power was obtained from the 27th and 28th sections of the Registration Act, 1868. Before the pass- ing of the Act Barristers had no such powers.—Mr. Swift said hp thought his Honour's view was the correct one. This concluded the revision proceedings, and the us- ual complimentary speeches were afterwards made.

div.p: THE CHILIAN WAR SEQUEL.
BALMACEDA COMMITS SUICIDE.

The " New 'York Herald" has received the following despatch from-Valparaiso, of Saturday's date "Ex-president Balmaceda shot himself in the temple in his room at the Argentine Legation in Santiago at half-past eight this morning. The news was received here this afternoon, and created the greatest excitement. The whole city is illuminated this evening, and sounds of rejoicing are heard everywhere. The latest intelligence from Santiago confirms and gives details of the suicide. It seems that -Balmaceda left Santiago on August 29, in the hope of escaping from Chili,but finding every retreat cut off, he returned thither on the 2nd inst., and went direct to the Argentine Legation. His intention had been to board the AltnErante Condell, which he expected to find at San Antonio Bay, and he was much chagrined to find that she had sailed. After his return to the Legation he was extremely nervous, and none but Senor Uriburu, the Argentine Minister,and another man whowas devoted to Balmaceda,were permitted to see him. Senor Uriburu went to the theatre yesterday evening, and on his return had a long talk with Balmaceda on the subject of the latter's ideas, which had previously been broached, about the advisability of surrender to the Junta. Both retired at midnight. Some time after eight o'clock this morn- ing Senora Uriburu heard a pistol shot in Balmaceda's bedroom, and notified the fact to her husband, who ran Ito the house of Senor Carla Martinez and brought him 'to the Legation. When the door of Balmaceda's room had been forced open they entered, and found the ex- President's body, still warm, with a gaping wound in the temple. The body was undressed and lay on the bed, the right hand holding a revolver. Senor Torro, Balmaceda's brother-in-law and Uruguayan minister, soon afterwards reached the house. The Junta was in- formed, and a commissioxt, comprising Senores Martinez, , Melchoir, and Concho, and Judge Aguerra, of the 1 Supreme Court, was immediately, appointed to proceed ' to the Legation and view the body. They there drew up a proces 'verbal certifying the facts. The German Minister accompanied the commission as an old friend of Balmaceda. The excitement in Santiago was indes- cribable. Great crowds gathered in front of the Lega- tion cheering and hooting continually, apparently quite frenzied over the death of the ex-President. Balmaceda left a letter for his mother. In a letter to Senor Uriburu, Balmaceda says : "When I saw that persecution was directed against me by persons who had once supported my administration, I concluded that the only way to end the persecution was to take my life, as I was the responsible one. Good-bye, true friend. Give my farewell to my wife and children. The Press Association is informed by Mr. Rose, con- fidential agent of the present Chilian Government in ;London, that news was received on Monday by the Chilian authorities in London confirming the report that ex-President Balaceda had committed suicide. A SECRET BURIAL. VALPARAISO, WEDNESDAL—The body of Senor Balma- ceda was buried secretly on the evening of the day on which he committed suicide. Every precaution was taken to prevent it from becoming known that the burial was about to take place. After Balmaceda had obtained an asylum at the Argentine Legation he demanded that he should be confined under the protection of the Provi- sional Government, and his removal to prison was fixed for the 19th inst.

div.head: HOLLOWAY TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE HOLLOWAY TRAGEDY.

On Wednesday Dr. Wynn Wostcott resumed, at Hollo- way, the inquest Upon the bodies of Ernest Nightingale, his wife, Elizabeth, their son, Ernest Arthur, aged 16 months, and their intant daughter, Ruby Florence, the three first of whom were found dead in bed from the effects of poison, whilst the latter died subsequently under the mysterious circumstances already reported. A great deal of evidence wns given to show that the deceased /man, who last year received nearly £4OO from his employer, a manufacturing chemist, by 'wayl/2 of salary and commission, had incurred liabilities of over £260, and had also borrowed £2OO from his father-in-lavv Some of the witnesses stated that the deceased man had also latterly taken to drink, whilst the house was only partly famished. There was only 16d. to his credit at the bank, and only 18d. was found in the house. The jury returned a verdict that the wife and elder child were murdered by the administration of prussic acid by Mr. Nightingale, who afterwards committed suicide whilst temporarily insane, caused by financial worry ; and that the baby Ruby, died from Qxhaustion, following convul- sions.

CHAT OPEN CAN OF POWDER.
The following paragraph is quoted from ft book written by one of the'most eminent physicians In 'Eng-
land. Read it once, twice, thrice, until you have thoroughly mastered the idea; then read the rest of this article.

Here it is clear as spring water, plain as a pipe stem. He says t All our familiar diseases—gout, rheumatism, bronchitis, pneumonia, pleurisy, asthma, insanity, epilepsy, never attack a healthy individual, but are the remitter existing disease, and are developed, NEVER. PRO- DUCIM, by some straiit on the system. " There! that will be a revelation to most people, and it otght to teach them a little practical wisdom. • No*, to show the application of this theory, take the 'case of Mrs. Harriett Steele, or 25, Sudeley-street, Isling- ton, London. She says: "Seven years ago I had an' attack of rheumatic fever, and was confined to my bed for two years. I had pain all over me which, of course, broke my sleep. Two physicians attended me. At times I I became insensible front the pain. After the fever left me I was quite prostrate and had dreadful pains in my limbs and through my chest and shoulders. After a time several pieces of deceased bone were taken from my wrist. Even liquid food, which was all I could take; gave me great distress. I got weaker and weaker, and feared I should be a cripple for life. I had to be lifted in and out of bed. One day a leaflet was left at my house telling of cases of cure in ailments like mine from the use of Mother Seigel's Syrup. I bought a bottle,and after taking half its contents I felt great relief, and be- gan to sit up, a thing I had not done for two years. Continuing the use of the Syrup I grew stronger, on account of the food which it enabled me to eat and•digest. After a while I was able to go out in an invalid chair,and by the time I had taken six bottles I could go about as usual, and have never had aehe or pain since'. y consent
to the publication of this statement in hope it maybe' useful to other sufferers."

Now this story sounds like a romance, and some may hesitate to accept it as truth. Yet it is both true and easy to understand if we look at it in the light of the paragraph we ask you to read three times. Like all other diseases, rheumatism is caused by poverty and impurity of the blood. The impurity consists of ari acid. poison produced by fermented and undigested food in the stomach and bowels, something existing for years before any serious harm seems to arise from it. It is like an open can of powder, safe enongh so long as no fire drops into it. But the time comes when exposure, wet feet, cold, or carelessness of some sort brings on a crisis Then there is trouble, in the shape of some particular malady—rheumatism, bronchitis, pneumonia, consuMp-, tion, or some other painful and perhaps fatal ailment. Do you see? Well, if you do, you comprehend why Mother Seigel's Syrup cures when other medicines and treatment are of no more use than putty to mend a A.

hole in a water-pipe. The idea is this: Mother Seigel's Syrup goes straight to the root of the' matter. It expels the poison from the blood, clears out the ashes and clinkers from the great human furnace (the stomach and bowels), and so leaves nothing for the disease to feqd on. That's the whole secret, and that's why it s!t Mrs. Steele on her feet when she feared there was no help for her. The moral is, don't spend time and money hammering at the symp- tons of disease ; don't languish and suffer for years while ignorant men practice on your credulity and try experiments on your tortured body ; let Mother Seigel abolish the indigestion and dyspepsia in which all the trouble lies, and become once more that credit to God and your country—a healthy man or woman through and through.
DETERMINED' SUICIDE AT CULCHiTIL

On Saturday morning, Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquiry at the Raven Inn, Culcheth, near Warrington, relative to the death of Richard Clarke, forty-five years of age, a cotton weaver, of Farley Common. Culcheth. The deceased was a single man,and resided with James Wall,a labourer, in a cottage. Last Wednesday week,Wall left home about eight o'clock in the morning, leaving the _deceased in bed. Wall returned about ten o'clock in the evening, and be was then the worse for drink.' He went upstairs to bed without striking a light. On stepping into bed,he felt the deceased's arm, and ; found it was quite cold. He spoke to him, but got no reply. He became alarmed, and ran out and called some neighbours. Police Constable Leeming, who was near the place at the time, also went up- stairs, and he found the deceased lying on his back on the bed, quite dead. He had a gunshot wound behind his right ear, and the skull was completely blown away. A gun which belonged to Wall was lying on the body, with the muzzle near the held, and the stock between the feet. A string was at- tached to .the trigger of the gun, and the other end was wrapped tightly round deceased's right hand. It was evident he had reclined on the bed, held the stock with his feet, and pulled the trigger by means of a string.—The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide whilst temporarily insane."

THE WARRINGTON TECHNICA.L INSTITUTE. INTRODUCTORY LECTURE. lii conneedon with the newly-formed Warrington Technical Institute, Mr. F. G. Ruddock, F.1.C., who has been appointed lecturer on chemistry and metal- lurgy, gave a lecture at the Museum on "Carbon," on Monday night. There was a large attendance. Mr. F. Monks, chairman of the Museum, Library, Arts, and Technical Instruction Committee, pre- sided. The Chairman, in his opening remarks, said they were met together that night to begin the work of their new Technical Institute. Many of them had Song been anxious to see such an Institute established is. order that the 'young of both sexes should have an opportunity of con- tinuing the education begun in most cases in their ele- mentary schools. At first they only proposed to make provision for evening classes and should watch the results with great interest and with the hope that they would be such as to encourage the Committee to go a step further in the direction of establishing day ',classes also. Their scheme, as swill, was complete, and the thought he might venture to suggest to his fellow townsmen that he thought there was a -splendid opening for the establishment of a high-class school for both sexes, which should embrace all the subjects required to be taught for a classical, corn- meicial, and domestic education. -He thought it was a misfortune that girls could not getn high-class education without having to go, as many did, to the high schools of Liverpool or Manchester. or tosome other school far away from their own homes. It was a condition of things that ought not to exist lipa town with 54,000 in- habitants,and with a well endowed Grammar School, ori- ginally intended to meet the educational requirements of their town and neighbourhood. lit was a question open for serious consideration whether their Grammar School could not be so assisted, devslloped, and reformed, and brought into such a position as to meet on all sides the higher education of Warrington and its neighbourhood. He knew some of the difficulties that might possibly stand in the way, but the time had come for reforma- tion in these matters, and asplendid opportunity offered itself for placing the higher education of the town upon a 'footing that should yield more satisfactory results and upon a more permanent and efficient basis than was 'possible under existing conditions. One thing was certain—that the responsibility for this higher education was now thrown upon the municipality itself, and Parliament had given full power to meet its require- ments, either by reforming existing institutions or establishing new ones that should meet the wants of its inhabitants; and the Technical Instruction Committee, in his opinion, would fail in its duty if it did not press , that question to a satisfactory settlement. The object I and scope of their work was that every, young person of , both sexes, should be able to continue their higher education under -such conditions as should ensure them the best methods of instruction under properly qualified teachers; and, as far as possible, the instruction should embrace such subjects as came within the range of a liberal and technical eduction in art, science, and other kindred subjects. In making that provision they were not unmindful of what was required from the students beyond a regular attendance. Knowledge did not come without effort, steady and persevering. Much could be done by a teacher in the methods he adopted of impart- ing knowledge,but sue Pss in anything had to be worked for, and the goal must be steadily kept in view. He had no doubt they should have many who would join the classes and give up in despair, or become so discouraged as to lose heart, and fall away into that indifference which is characteristic of the multitude. He hoped, however, that there would be many who, already feeling the pleasures and advantages of education, desire to con- tinue those habits of thought which sought to develope the faculties with which they -were endowed, and which, when so developed, gave to life such pleasure and useful- ness. They might depend upon it that the greatest happiness came from within rather than from without. Mere external circumstances might or might not be a source of pleasuro,'but the healthy exercise of the mind, of the trained habit of thought which understood much that it saw revealed in nature was dependent only on those hidden sources of joy which sprang from the cul- tivation of those faculties with which God had abund- antly endowed both rich and poor alike. To the student who sought to more thoroughly understand the business , or profession he intended to follow the Institute offered very considerable advantages. Whether in art, sciences, languages, or commerce they would find suitable provi- sion in those branches which might materially affect their future welfare. To all, therefore, whether rich or poor, wise or simple, young or old, the institute offered advantages of no mean importance ; and to the indus- trious with more than average ability, it opened up a prospect of advancement and real happiness which would certainly be a blessing to the individual if rightly used, and possibly of great advantage to the town itself in its development as an industrial and commercial centre. It seemed to him at times that their youth was more inclined to be an athlete than a student, but it was the duty of the citizens to provide for both health of mind and body leaving to individual tastes and inclin- ations the choice between the two. To his mind they should go hand in hand, and it would appear that winter, with its long cold nights, afforded a natural inclination to study, just as summer with its warmth and newness of life offered inducements to outdoor sports and amusements. The establishment of a tech- nical institute and the opening of a gymnasium would mark a distinct advance in the progress of thetown,and it would rest with the young to determine their value and usefulness amongst them as educational influences of a high character, promoting the best interests of the town and neighbourhood. (Applause.) Mr. Ruddock then gave his lecture on "Carbon,". the lecture being made very interesting by several curious experiments, which were successfully performed.
THE "FREEMAN'S JOURNAL" MANIFESTO.

The" Freeman's Journal ",nf Tuesday morning, in the : eourse of a long article, says —" When the hopes of the conntry are high, and the outside world has begun to recognise that the Irish nation is a force worth respecting, some matter of detail oz of self arises. Passions are in- flamed, and the bond of union is broken. This has hap- pened to-day, and one man has caused it all. It is abso- lutely necessary that the independence of the Irish Par- liamentary party be maintained. Independence does not, however, imply perpetual antagonism. Indepen- dent support and independent alliance may be useful as independent opposition. It would be madness to oppose any party in the act of conceding Irish rights. If the Irish people must be united to be strong, the man who stands between our people, and union must be content to be regarded as a foe. The man is Mr. Charles Stewart Parnell. The public spirit which will secure national union is the best and only real guarantee of our Parlia- mentary independence.
Seven passengers and four officials have been killed and a number of persons severely injured by a railway collision at Golaczowy, on the Russo-German frontier.
THE CHESHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY. PROPOSED MEETING AT WARRINGTON. _

On Wednesday a-fiern—oon it--meeting convened by the Mayor, was held in the Council Chamber of the Warrington Town Hall, for the purpose of consider- ing the advisability of inviting the Cheshire Agri- cultural Society to hold their annual exhibition of 1892, in Warrington. The M‘yor (Alderman Fran- comb) presided, and there were also present Mr. J. C. Parr, Mr. G. Greenall, Mr. J. Warburton, Mr. T. S. Burgess, Mr. IL A. Naylor, Mr. B. Melville, Captain Withington, Mr. C. Greenall. Mr. J. Thompson, and Mr. Stanley Wilson. _

The MAYOR said he received last week a long and care- fully written letter from Mr. Collin Mclver asking if it would not be wise to try to get the Cheshire Agricul- tural Society to hold their meeting at Warrington next year. Ile believed there was another town in Cheshire which was very anxious to have the agricultural meet- ing, but Mr. Mclver thought that if they approached the Society and showed they meant business it would One to Warrington. He might say that after receiving the letter from Mr. ' Mclver he had a visit from Mr. Gilbert Greenall, and he, together with Mr: Melville, urged upon him the necessity of calling a meeting and showed the advantage that it would be to the people of Warrington, if they could have bhe Society's meeting here. He was anxious to do anything he could to bring money into the town, and consequently he was only too pleased to issue that circular. He hoped that, although they had not a large meeting, they should be successful in getting the show there next year. (Hear, hear.) He then read letters of apology for non-attendance from Mr. John White Mr. C. L. Evans (Runcorn), Mr. Stapleton Bretherton White, Mr. James Tinsley, Mr. Mclver, Mr. J. E. Davies, and Mr. J. Marson. All these gentle- men spoke in favour of the show being held at War- rington. Mr. J. C. Parr thanked the Mayor for calling that meeting. He thought the interests of the town would be very much promoted if it were possible to get the Cheshire Agricultural Society to have their meeting at Warrington. He had just been asking if the society ever held its show out of Cheshire as there was no part of Warrington now in Cheshire. Mr. rg. S. Burgess said that in 1873 the show was held in Sankey-st., opposite the Town Hall. 1 The Mayor said he understood that the whole of War- rington was only out of Cheshire for the purposes of the Local Government Act, 1888, but for some purposes part of it was still in Cheshire. Some conversation then ensued as to a suitable site for the show, and other matters. Mr. Gilbert Greenall suggested that there was an excellent site opposite the police station at Stockton Heath. The Mayor said the fields near St. James Church would be an excellent place if there was no fear of their being Under floods. Mr. Parr asked what was the usual guarantee the society expected, and Mr. Melville replied that £250 was a sum which had been mentioned as likely to tempt the society, though it would be better if they could mention a higher. The Mayor said he understood the society wanted £250, a field of ten acres, and a supply of water to the field. Mr. T. S. Burgess pointed out that the field mentioned at Stockton Heath, though about two miles from the Cen- tral Station, was only about one mile from Latchford Station, and probably the new road to the station would be opened by the time the show was held. It was then decided to appoint a small committee to meet the Agri- • cultural Society and ascertain their requirements. The.. Committee was then appointed as follows :—Mr. G. Greenall, Mr. C. Mclver, Mr. J. E. Davies, Mr. Lister Kaye, Mr. C. Greenall, Mr. H. Milling, and Mr. W. Jones. The meeting was then adjourned.

div.p: RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN SPAIN.
SEVEN LIVES LOST

MADRID, THURSDAY. —A railway accident attended with a loss of life, occurred to-day at Burgos, where an express train from San Sebastian, while travelling at a high rate of speed, came into collision with a mixed train. Seven persons were killed outright, and a number were injured-14 seriously.

div.head: WRECK OF A. LIVERPOOL BARQUE.
div.p: WRECK OF A. LIVERPOOL BARQUE.
TWELVE MEN LOST.

A " Times " second edition Calcutta telegram, 'of Thursday says :—Advices, dated the Bth inst., from Melbourne. states that the barque Fiji, loaded with dynamite, bound from Liverpool to Melbourne, was wrecked on the Victoria coast near Port Campbell, on the 6th inst.; and that, while attempting to land by the life line, twelve of her crew were drowned.
THE MANCHESTER. PALACE OF VARIETIES. LIQUOR LICENCE REFUSED.

-- - Extraordinary interest was manifested at:Manchester, on Thurstlay, in regard to an application by the Palace of Varieties for a licence for the sale of intoxicating liquor, made on behalf of the management by Mr. Gully, Q.C., M.P., previously granted by the licensing com- mittee. The justices refused to confirm the licence by a majority of forty to eighteen.

div.head: CHINA AND THE POWERS.
div.p: CHINA AND THE POWERS.

REBELLION SPREADING. CONCENTRATION OF WARSHIPS. NEW YORK, WEDNESDAY,—The New York Herald has received the following message from its correspondent at Shanghai :—" The situation is becoming worse. The disturbances at Ichang are growing, and are the prelude to other disorders. The valley of the Yanetse is in rebellion. Wuchang, the central seat of the Viceroy, is ready to revolt, and then the towns open to foreigners, Hankow and Chunting, are likely to follow. The latter town is difficult to defend by warships, owing to the shallowness of the river. Great excitement prevails and strangers are fleeing. Shanghai is among the threatened towns. Measures have been taken to despatch three ships of war to Wuchang, and the combined fleets are concentrating at Shanghai. M. Lemaire, the French Minister, has left here for Pekin."
