div.head: TRADES DEMONSTRATION
div.p: TRADES DEMONSTRATION
AT ST. HELENS.
PROCEESSION AND MEETING.

A demonstration and mass meeting of the whole of the trades in St. Helens was held in that town under the auspices of the St. Helens Trades Coun- cil on Saturday afternoon. Fortunately the pro- ceedings were favoured with fine weather, and the gathering was a great success. The members of the various trades assembled at their headquarters and marched to Hardshaw Fields, behind the Theatre Royal, where the officials and executive committee of the Trades Council arranged them in one united procession. The neighbourhood was animated by the presence of many thousands of demonstrators and their friends, and these coupled with numerous brass bands,fiying colours and banners,and thorough- fares crowded with interested spectators were clear evidence that the working-men of the town were having a real" day out." About half-past two the procession moved on its journey. It was headed by a carriage containing Mr. Tom Mann,of London, president of the DOckers' Union and one of the Rcyal Commissioners on Labour; Mr. Samuel Woods president of thr Lancashire Miners' Federation and Labour candidate for the Ince Division; Mriv& Mear, organising secretary of the Amalgamat4 Society of Railway Servants; Mr. Jenkins, general secretary of the Bakers' Society; local trade leaders and representatives of the Liverpool and Warrington Trade Councils. First came the miners, headed by the Parr Brass Band; next came the Glass Bottlemakers' Society, with the Earlestown Viaduct Brass Band at their head; then followed in order the coopers headed by the Borough Brass Band, operative bricklayers, carpenters and joiners headed by the York- street (St. Helens) Brass Band, house painters and decorators plasterers, railway servants, cloggers, plate- glass workers beaded by the Sutton-road Wesleyan Brass Band, bakers and confectioners with the Platt Bridge Brass Band, plumbers, life assurance agents, Typograp- hical Society members, sheet-glass fiatteners, engine winders, engine and boiler men, builders' labourers, amalgamated tailors, wheelwrights and blacksmiths, St. Helens Labour Union members, and marquee and sheet makers. The demonstrators marched along Hall-street, Church-street', Bridge-street, %Liverpool-road, Westfield- street, Peter-street, Boundaly-road, Duke-street, and Corporation-street. On their arrival at Hardshaw-fields an open-air meeting was held near Birchley-street. Councillor Robert Hunter' president of the St. Helens Trades Council, occupied the chair, and he was sup- ported by Mr. Tom Mann, London; Mr. Samuel Woods, Wigan ; Mr. Mear, Liverpool ; Mr. Jenkins, Liverpool ; Mr. W. S. Potter and Mr. E. Carney, Liver- pool Trades Council ; Mr. William Bullock and Mr. John Price, Warrington Trades Council ; Mr. Sexton, Liverpool Labourers' Electoral Association ; Mr. James Hunter, St. Helens Glass Bottlemakers ; Mr. H. Ellard, vice-president St. Helens Trades Council; Mr. T. Glover, miners' agent and secretary to the council ; Mr. John Bradbury, president St. Helens Plateglass Workers; Mr. W. Battersby, miners, kc. The Chairman said he thought the great demenstration they had made must be very satisfactory to the officials of the Trades Council. They had shown by their proceedings that day that they were determined to make the labour interest felt still more throughout the town. ' (Applause.) Mr. T. Glover (secretary)then read several letters of apology for non-attendance, including one from Sir Charles Nike, who promised to attend on a more convenient date. Mr. F. A. Chancing, M.P., for East Northamptonshire, wrote that he was doing all he could to promote the orpr,anisation of labour and the attainment of -better conditions of life for the working classes; Mr. W. Alatkin, secretary of the general union of joiners. Councillor T. R. Threl- fell, of Southport, and Mr. Wallace Revill, who had pro- mised the use of the Theatre Royal, free of charge, for the public meeting in case of wet weather. He went on to speak of the object of that gathering, and traced the history of the Trades Council in 'S t. Helens. It was, he said, only by working shoulder to shoulder and strength- ening their organisation that the working classes could be better clothed, better cared for, and become better citizens of the town in which they lived. (Applause.) Mr. Henry Ellard (St. Helens) moved—" That this meeting is of opinion that the time has arrived when there should be more representatives :of labour in town councils, boards of Guardians, and all local bodies, and this meetinc, pledges itself to support those candidates whom theerades Council may bring forward." He asked them to sink their political differences, and vote for the men who would further their interests. (Applause.) Mr. James Hunter (St. Helens), seconded the resolu-

tion. Mr. Richard Story (Warrington), supported the reso- lution and asserted that the "upper ten "and the upper classes had too long held the power in this country. They had, he said, furthered their own interests, and it was now for the working classes to use the power given them by the franchise to bring about an improvement —socially, morally, and spiritually. An individual in the cr3wd occasioned some disorder, and Mr. Story caused great laughter by remarking that if the individual in question had not opened his mouth they should not have known there was a fool present. Mr. J. G. Costain (Liverpool) also supported the reso- tion which was carried unanimously. The Chairman stated that the Trades Council had de- cided to bring out two labour candidates at the ensuing municipal election, namely Mr. T. Glover, miners' agent, in Hardshave Ward, and Mr. Henry Ellard in Eccleston Ward. _

Mr. Battersby (St. Helens) proposed "That in the opinion of this meeting the time has arrived when a general eight hours' working day ought to be established by law in all trades where a majority of the organised members, voting by ballot, is in favour of the same, and this meeting pledges itself to do all in its power to bring about this result." _ _ _
John Bradbury (St. Helens) seconded the resolu- tion. _ .

Mr. S. Woods (Wigan) supported the resolution. He ventured to affirm that the adoption of a measure of eight hours per day for the working-men of the country was within a measurable distance of becoming an accom- plished fact. The only opponents were, on the one hand, the employers, and on the other hand some old fossilised trade unionists who could not get out of the groove in which they were born. (Laughter and applause). The working-men of the country must work unitedly until they had brought about that ideal of which they had long thought, eight hours work, eight hours play, eight hours rest, and eight "bob" a day. (Applause.) Mr. Tom Mann also supported the resolution, and was received with prolonged cheers. He was thoroughly in accord with the opinions expressed by preceding speakers as to the advantages to be derived by working-men mak- ing use of municipal and other institutions towards the advancement and improvement of their interests. The time had gone by for their dependence upon employers or philanthropy, and it was for them to work out their own social salvation. St. Helens, with its 13,000 or 14.000 of working-men, had done well hitherto' but she had not done enough. He regretted to hear that the Amalgamated Engineers, of which society he was a member, and that the chemical and copper workers, in whose welfare he had a deep and personal interest, had not joined the Trades Council, and he exhorted them to try and close their ranks and so still further strengthen the cause of labour in that town. (Applause.) Reflec- tions upon many of the conditions of life and labour of the poorer classes had caused him to revolt, and he had revolted once and for all, and he stood there, openly declaring himself a determined rebel—determined to rebel against the forces that surrounded the workers of this country, and tied them down to degradation with all its nasty concomitants. (Cheers.) The physiological law of having food must be complied with, and he was therefore determinedly opposed to the chaos that existed in the industrial systems of to-day. No economist and no capitalist in the country could defend the position that it was necessary to have poverty, and believing; that, he bad laid himself out to' work and to con- tinue to work in his endeavour to destroy poverty, and he held it to be the most sacred duty of any, man to banish poverty from the land. (Cheers.) He pointed out the excessively long hours worked by many men in St. Helens and elsewhere, and aitributed many of the evils suffered by workmen to the fact that each man under present conditions did two men's work for the pay of elle. In endeavouring to bring about the needed reforms they must drop their political partisanship and devote their energies to the organisation of the great labour party. He had bright hopes as to the future of the labour molvement, and trades unionism in the end would not only benefit them individually, but would add to the strength of the country. He wished "good luck" to the people of St. Helens, and hoped the Trades Council would grow and develop to the furthest possible extent. (Loud cheers.) Mr. A. Mear moved the third resolution, "That seeing the great good that has been done by trades unions dur- ing the past few years in bettering the condition of the working classes generally, this meeting calls upon all those who are not in any union to become united at once, and then strilngthen their position by becoming members of the St. Helens Trade Council." (Applause.) Mr. John Price seconded, and the resolution was carried. Votes of thanks were tendered to the speakers and the chairman, and the meeting terminated. A CONTINGENT FROM WARRINGTON.

In connection with the demonstration about 20 mem- bers of the Warrington Bratieh of the Baker's Union, journeyed by 'bus to St. Helens, leaving the head- quarters, the Roe Buck Hotel, at 1.30 p.m. on Saturday. After taking part in the procession,they were entertained to dinner at the George Hotel, by their St. Helens breth- ren the caterer being Mr. Boardman, and about 50 sitt- ing down. Mr. McNiven occupied the chair,and gave an excellent address on the pro,ress of the Amalgamated Union. Mr. Ware and Mr. Nimmo, of Warrington, suit- ably replied, Mr. Nimmo speaking of the brotherly love that should be extended one to another in furthering the cause of unionism. The remainder of the evening was spent in singing, songs being contributed by Messrs.
Rabbit, Barnes, Rathbone, Leigh, and others. The re- turn journey was commenced at 10 p.m.,Warrington be- ing reached soon after 11.,a1l having thoroughly enjoyed themselves.
WARRINGTON ADJOURNED BREWSTER SESSIONS. - ,

The adjourned Brewster Sessions were held at the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, before the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Francomb), Aldermen Burgess and Holmes, Councillor James Fairclough, Captain Ridgway, and Messrs. F. Monks, and E. J. Guest. At the principal Brewster Sessions appli- cations for new licenses were made by Joseph Houghton Clarke, for a new hotel in Battersby- lane, by Mr. Wm. Bolton for a full license house at 112 and 114 Battersby-lane, Mrs. Susan Lawton for a full alehouse license for the Grove House,Bewsey- road ; and Mr. Henry Corney for an off-license to sell beer and cider at 173 Orford-lane. All these applications were adjourned till the next licensing day (last Tuesday) but, as will be seen. none of them were again made except that of Mr. Corney.
APPLICATION TOR A BEER AND CIDER LICENSE.

Henry Corney made a fourth application for a license to sell beer and cider to be consumed off the premises, at 173 Orford-lane. Mr. Browns, solicitor, appeared be oppose the application on behalf of Mr. George Walker, manager of the Battersby-lane Carriage Works, and a number of other inhabitants of the district.—Mr. Corney presented a petition in support of his application, signed by over 150 residents of the upper part of Orford-lane. He said he had just completed 38 years' service in the army, and hoped the magistrates would be good enough to grant him the license, so that he might make a main- tenance for himself and become a citizen of Warrington. —By Mr. Browne: He kept a provision shop and the beerhouse would be an accessory to that if required.— Mr. Clarke had an out-door beer license on the other side, but the increase of the inhabitants of the upper part of Orford-lane necessitated another. Then there was Mr. Brown's out-door license 600 yards off, Taylor's 400yds., and the Hawthorne beerhouse 50 yards further. The nearest one going through Dickinson-st. and down Battersby-lane was about 600 yds. There was a canteen at the barracks.—Mr. Byrne said he lived in a smallshop at the corner of Barrack Gate, and had measured the distance to Mr. Clarke's, which was about 460 yards, That was the nearest house, and the next was at the oorner of Sharpe-st:, down Battersby-lane; 600 yards off. The next nearest was the Cemetery Inn. As for the canteen at the barracks that was only for military men, and it was no use Mr. Browne mentioning that. The district was growing very much. There were houses springing up by fifties every month. He considered the license was necessary.—By Mr. Browne : Witness was formerly in the army. Clarke's house was 360 yards from witness's shop and about 120 yards from the applicant's.—Mr. Hackett, 197, Orford-lane, one of the petitioners, said he had signed because he considered the license necessary. He had noticed great difficulty in getting the customers served between 12-30 and 1 p.m on Sundays at Clarke's. On other days there was plenty of convenience, but the trouble was getting there.—Mr. Caradise, 2, Dickinson-street, said the nearest place to his house to get beer was Clarke's, and when he went there for his supper beer there was always a great crush. —Mr. Browne said he could produce evidence that the license was not required. He had nothing whatever to say against Mr. Corney's character; he did not suppose anyone in Warrington had a better, but he asked their woiships not to look upon the question as one of character, and as a matter of a man having served his colours and his country for 38 years and wanting to provide for himself, after retiring from the army, but would ask them whether they had not fully realised that these outdoor licenses were far more dangerous than the fully licensed public-houses.—John Houghton, 162, Forster-street, said his house was about a stone's throw from Mr. Corney's, and in his opinion there was no necessity for any new license, but the neighbourhood was amply supplied. —The Mayor: Are you a teetotaller ?—Mr. Houghton: It so happens that I am.—The Mayor: Then it won't matter to you whether there is any house there or not.—James Gandy, owner of considerable property in the district, including his own residence,which is right opposite to Mr. Corney's cansidered there was no necessity for a license.—Asked by Mr. Corney whether he was a teetotaller, he objected to answer the question unless the Bench desired it.— Alderman Burgess thought it ought not to be put.—The Magistrates' Clerk said the question was admissible, and Mr. Gandy then said he was a teetotaller, though he did not object as such, but as a resident and an owner.— John Gandy, shopkeeper in Leonard-st., close to Mr. Corney's, thought the license was unnecessary. He was a teetotaller, and he considered that if there should be any increase of those places the chances were that there would be a good deal of competition, and supplying women with drink and having, it put down as groceries. , —Richard Storey, 160 Orford-lane, thought there was sufficient accommodation in the neighbourhood. The only time there was any push at all was at dinner time on Sundays.—Mr. Corney: Of all the persons who have given evidence thereis not one on the upper side where all these houses are built.—The Mayor: It does not matter. They don't drink beer.—Mr. Corney said Mr. Storey was the only person he called on with the peti- tion, who said he was an abstainer.—The Bench con- sidered in their retiring-room for about ten minutes,and on their return the Mayor announced that they had de- ' cided not to grant the license.

REPAIRS TO THE ROYAL EXCHANGE INN.

fCouncillor Wm. Bolton, applied as the owner of the Royal Exchange Inn, for permission to alter the construc- tion of one of the rooms, by lowering the floor and putt- ing in a window. He merely mentioned the matter in order that the Bench might be aware of it at the next application for renewal of licenses.--Chief Constable Hunt said the alterations would be an improvement and would involve no enlargement.—The request was ac- ceeded to.
DROWNING FATALITY AT EARLES- TO WN.

On Tuesday night, shortly after eight o'clock, a boy named Walter Sankey, eleven years of age, son of Hugh Sankey, of the lock house, Newton Com- mon Locks, Earlestown, was accidently drowned by falling into the locks immediately opposite his father's house. The unfortunate lad had earlier on in the night crossed the canal by the swing bridge to his brother's house on the opposite side of the canal, and shoitly before eight o'clock returned home, with his brother's wife. He then went to the back of the house to break sticks and gather coal. after which be asked if he naight return to his brothers. Permission was given him to do so, and he left the house for that purpose. Since he last crossed the canal a flat had approached the locks, and the horse driver had turned the swing bridge, preparatory to the boat enter- ing the locks. The lad was not aware of this, and the night being very dark, he did not perceive his danger and walked into the locks. In his fall it was supposed his head came into contact with something, rendering him unconscious, as no cry was heard. The horse driver however, heard the splash and raised an alarm,and John. Sankey seeing a cap on the water, jumped in, but could see nothing of his brother. Search was then made, and the body was recovered shortly afterwards but life was extinct.
INQUEST.

An inquest on the body was held at the Ship Inn, on Thursday, by Mr. S. Brighouse,coroner:—Hugh Sankey, father of the deceased lad, stated he was away from home at Garston when the accident occurred,and he did not return home until midnight, when his son was dead. He said he did not know that there was any obligation on the flat men or horse drivers to notify those at the lock house when a boat was approaching. It had never been done during the 30 years he had rpided there. On very many occasions he had saved people from drown- ing when the bridge had been off. The Coroner said they hardly needed any evidence to show this was a dangerous place. They required a lamp very close to the bridge.—John Sankey, said the first he knew of his brother being in the water, was the alarm raised by the horse driver. He saw the cap in the water and jumped in thinking it was the body, but found it was only the cap. He got out of the lock again and the .body was' then recovered by a boat hook. He thought they should, have a light on each side of the canal. The ques— tion had been brought up many a time, and tte Commissioners had put two lamps at • the top, of the hill, close together, where they were not needed. In his opinion the accident would not have happened had a lamp been there.—Thomas Rowles, horse driver, gave evidence as to his turning the bridge, and hearing a splash.—The Coroner said it was for the jury to say if the case was accidental, and what should be done to prevent any case of the kind in future. The bridge was bound to be turned off from time to time,and when it was off, the place was dangerous to the public. The owners of the canal ought to take some steps to remove that danger, and they could include such a sug- gestion in their verdict. The jury then returned a ver- dict that deceased came by his death accidentally, and they recommended that, for the better protection of life in the future, the turn bridge and approaches, thereto, should be better lighted. They suggested that the Board of Commissioners for Newton, and the London and North-Western Railway Company, should be communi- cated with, and be asked to immediately carry out the suggested lighting.—The Coroner promised to transmit the recommendation to the clerk to the Commissioners and solicitor to the Railway Company.

He said : It is indispensable, if there is to he any re- awakening ot village life, if there is to be any rais- ing up of the manhood of the villages, it is indis- pensable that you should have popular bodies in the villages which must have the management of their own charities—the management of allotments under the Act—powers overpublic buildings, over common land, and power over the compulsory acquisition of land for public objects. A proposal such as this is in strange contrast with the jeers of Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH, who first tells his countrymen that "every simple parish in England had a parish vestry," and then says the people do not go to the parish vestry" be- cause the parish vestry has nothing to do." Was there ever such a confession of ineptitude No- thing to do Precisely, and that is why legislation is needed; a parish, like a municipality, requires to be put in a position to manage its own affairs. It needs Home Rule on a small scale; but when the Liberals tried to induce the present Administra- tion to proceed with reform:in this direction, they would have none of it. div.head: "TOTJCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOTJCH AND GO."

The Nationalists are determined to stand by-the evicted tenants, whether Mr. Parnell will help or not with the Paris Fund. He seems to have thought he could" put the screw on" by keeping the money locked up ; but he will fail. It was resolved, on Tuesday, at a meeting of the Irish Federation that there should be a special appeal for funds; and there is every reason to believe that funds will be forthcoming.

-- The latest news from Spain is to the effect that about 1,000 lives have been lost in consequence of the terrible floods. Great is the misery of the homeless survivors, and subscriptions for their relief are being opened in London, and in the oapitals of the continent. But why not extend the aid ? Kindly hearts are not confined to capital eities. The Mayors of provincial towns ought to open and head additional subscription lists.

In appointing the new Postmaster General,Lord Salisbury has evidently been thinking less of the likeliest man than of the safest seat. However, the Liberals of East Manchester mean to contest the return of Sir James Fergusson, and have an excellent candidate in Mr. C. P. Scott, editor of the" Manchester Guardian." They can scarcely hope to win ; but they mean to try; and that is the spirit in which every Tory seat should be contested • at the General Election.

_ The Tories of Warrington have for some time laid the flattering unction to their souls that no Liberal candidate could be found, because the Committee of Selection have been in no haste to commit them- selves or the party. It is no secret amongst Liberals that in case of a bye-election a candidate would be immediately forthcoming; and it is not too .much to say that such arrangements are in pro- gress as will ensure a good candidate at the General Election. Can the Tories say as much? They talk about their various " Richmonds ;" but it does not appear that any one of them is ready to enter the field.
Jacques has succeeded in his self-imposed task •of fasting 50 days. Presumably—to parody a well-known couplet—

The jingling of the guineas Heals the hurt the stomach feels. If his body is lighter, his pocket is heavier, and he has survived the experiment. It is stated that he was escorted home by some thousands of per- sons—more than would have attended his funeral if he had succumbed. Nothing succeeds like ,sturness.

Joseph Skinner, who is described as a forgeman, was fined, on Monday, by the Warrington magis- trates,for being drunk and disorderly. Drunk as he was, he sought to be "more so ;" and tried on what is known as "the circus trick." He pre- tended to be in a fit, and called for brandy. "No more brandy, no more fits," says the clown, and that was Skinner's plan. But it didn't run to brandy, for a policeman ran to him, and a doctor -declared that he was shamming. There was one thing real, however, in the end—that was the fine of ten shillings.

In a letter to his congregation, the Rev. C. H. Spurgeon says :—" The Lord does not give half mercies; Ho will perfect that which concern° th us. Now He has heard prayer. Had I died, all infidelity would have noted it as a proof that prayer was useless. We have a right to score one on the other side." Isn't this pushing matters rather too far? What of other ministers who have been prayed for and have died? And what of men who have died at prayer meetings and in the pulpit? But perhaps Mr. Spurgeon thinks nobody counts in these matters except Mr. Spurgeon.

Be this as it may, the great Baptist preacher is certainly not in harmony with modern thought on this matter. Here is a case in point. On Black- pool sands, on Sunday, a local brother who has faith in prayer and collections gave his experience. He told how his wife stuck fast with her sewing machine? She had oiled it and done all she could; but it wouldn't go. Ho advised her to pray over it; she did, and, after that, "it went beautifully." And so did the congregation. Within two minutes of the tale being told, two-thirds of the audience had walked away. The story was too much for them.

The Rev. E. Bowser, Secretary of the Lanca- shire and Cheshire Union of Baptists, put not only his foot in it, hut went in overhead when he stated at an Earlestown recognition meeting, on Monday night, that "the question of baptism by immersion had been finally settled as tlae right interpretation of the Gospel." The Rev. T. Collins, Primitive Methodist, who was assisting in the recognition, declined to recognise the truth of the statement as to baptism. But he made his protest in such a way as to get himself into hot water. This was a mistake; he should have bantered his reverend brother on his liking for immersion and given him, so to speak, a cold douche. However the little scene settled one thing, and that is that baptism by immersion is• not "finally settled."

At the adjourned licensing sessions at War- rington, on Tuesday, the only application was for an off-license, and that was ultimately refused. Whilst evidence was being given, the Mayor (Aid. Francomb), took the extraordinary course of ask- ing a witness who opposed thc) license if he • was a teetotaller. Alderman Burgess very pro- perly remarked that such a question ought not to be put. He might have gone further, and said it was an impertinent question as coming from the Bench. What if one of the witnesses had asked the Mayor if he "liked a glass ?" And what (if the answer had been " Yes ") if the witness had suggested that he was not therefore fit to have a voice in a licensing case? Would his Worship not have thought that impertinent? The Mayor of Warrington has yet to learn that a man does not lose his rights as a citizen by becoming si, teetotaller.

We are informed that the Warrington Licensing Committee when they adjourned, on Tuesday, to decide on the application before them had under consideration the advisability of announcing that it was their intention, next year, to distribute some of the present licenses. They were acting ultra vires in discussing such a proposal on Tues- day. But to be forewarned is to be forearmed. Respectable people living in respectable neighbour- hoods will now know that, without their being consulted, there is a possibility of having a drink- shop thrust in their midst, by way of improving their manners and their morals, and enhancing the value of property! The right thing to do is to largely reduce the number of licensed houses. A new lease of life to the monopolists—in new neighbourhoods—will be an outrage on the community.

"Fame" is the title of a new "Journal for Advertisers." It is well-printed, and well edited, gives sound advice, and is altogether wide-awake. We append, by way of sample, a number of "Pro- verbs for Advertisers" : Believe not every tale of circulation. An advertisement is not a luxury, but a necessity. A timid advertiser bath little business. Give up thy shirt rather than thy advertisement. Take space when space is--, for space will away. The early advertiser retires healthy, wealthy, and wise. From trivial advertisements great orders oft arise. Despise not a small advertisement, a postal receipt, or a humble canvasser. Advertisements are the windows through which the smart business man looks out for trade. There's nothing so well-known but may be advertised. A smart agerdis a jewel to the advertiser. Incline thine ear unto the agent.

A LTRINCIIAM SHOW. The annual show of the Altrincham Agricultural Society was held on Thursday. There were about 3,000 entries of live and dead stock, and in the principal classes this was an advance upon the show of last year. A great number of visitors at- tended the show yard, including many from War- rington. At the annual luncheon Lord. Egerton,who was one of the speakers,expressed the hope that the Society would next year make a special feature of prizes for produce grown by farm labourers on allotments.
LOCAL NEWS.
A BOSE THAT BLOOMS Too OFTEN.

The notorious Rose Kelly is fast approaching the century in her appearances before the Widnes magistrates For the 83rd time she was brought up at Widnes Police Court on Monday, charged with -being drunk and dis- orderly, and in default of paving a line of 10s. and costs, she was sent to goal for 14 days hard labour.

RUNCORN POEMS COURT. At this Court on Wednesday before Mr. John Brun- drit, Louis Heutcoeur and Dennis Mullen were each fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly.—Ellen Coffey, a woman of bad character, made her 31st appear- ance and was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour for being guilty of disorderly conduct.—John Slater was charged with aiding and abetting the woman, and he was fined ss. and costs.—On Thursday before Mr. Brun- drit and Mr. C. Reynolds, William Corkhill was fined 103. and costs for assaulting P.C. Worth while in the execution of his duty, on the 21st inst. AUTUMN SHOW next Tuesday and Wednesday.—J. and W. PUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—ildvt. MARRIAGE OE MISS KNOWLES FORMERLY OF RUNCORN. On Tuesday afternoon, at St. Anne's Church, Stanley, near Liverpool, the marriage took place of Mr. Thomas Girling, of Zenobia Villa, Old Swan, to Edith Annie Knowles, daughter of Mr. John Knowles, of the Railway ' Hotel, Lime-street, Liverpool, and of Wilson's Hotel, Runcorn. After breakfast, the happy pair left Liverpool for London en route for the Isle of Wight, where the honeymoon will be spent. A number of friends from Runcorn wore present at the ceremony and the subse- quent proceedings, and the valuable presents were pleasing evidences of the respect and esteem in which the bride and bridegroom are held. PREMIER SAFETIES. Cash or Hire.—GARLAND. Warrington, —Advt.

div.head: ORDERS FOR PARENTS' MAINTENANCE.
div.p: ORDERS FOR PARENTS' MAINTENANCE.

Robert Massey was sum:coned to Runcorn Petty Ses- sions to show cause why he should not contribute to- wards the support of his mother.—Mr.Frodsham said the mother was chargeable at 3s. a week and three brothers now contributed to her support. The defendant was employed at Runcorn Soap and Alkali Works and his average wages were £1 14s. a week. The Guardians asked for an order of 6d. per week. The order was made.—Thomas Wyche was summoned by Mr. Frodsham fore]. 13s. 41. arrears of an order made upon him to support his father, who is chargeable to the Union. The ameunt was ordered to be paid in two months. ATTEMPTED OUTRAGE ON A WOMAN AT RUNCORN. A young man of rough appearance, named Michael Calligan, was brought up on remand at Runcorn Police Court on Tuesday, charged with unlawfully and indecently assaulting Ellen Flargrea,ves, a married woman, who lives in Heath-road. On Saturday night, about nine o'clock, the woman and her husband, Johnson Hargreaves, were returning home by way of Cemetery- fields. She was about 20 yards in advance of her hus- band and when she turned the corner of the houses the prisoner rushed at her, caught hold of her throat, threw her down, and committed the offence complained of. She screamed loudly and Hargreaves quickly came to her aid, but it was not until after a severe struggle that she was released from the ruffians grasp. The prisoner then ran away towards the chemical works but he was after- wards apprehended and identified. AUTUMN Snow next Tuesday and Wednesday.---J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-et., Warrington.--iltirt.

Hu/won* EvenzNa CLASSES. The evening classes, in connection with Runcorn School Board, which were so successful last winter, were re-opened last Monday evening in Greenway-road School. Although the weather was wet and stormy, fifty youths presented themselves as students and a highly satisfac- tory and large number for a first night. Besides the three It's, there will be taught at the classes, grammar, geography, algebra, mensuration and shorthand. Geo- graphy is a very popular part of the curriculum with those attending the classes and the magic lantern will be frequently brought into use in duplicating the geographi- cal peculiarities of the countries which will be dealt with by the teacher. There are about 20 students in the short- hand class. The head master, Mr. F. Moulton is assisted by a staff of assistants including Mr. W. Epps, Mr. W. Stubbing and Mr. F. Whalley.

A VIOLENT POLE AT WIDNIIS. Before Mr. Gossage and Mr. Timmis at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Joseph I3arroa, a Pole, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly and assaulted Tweddle and Scott and also damaged the cell. On Saturday night the constables apprehended the prisoner in Water-st., for being drunk and disorderly. The pri- soner was following an Irishman along the street and attempting to strike him NVith a quart bottle he carried. When the constables interposed he repeatedly struck and kicked them, and r•II arriving at the police station he threw himself on the floor and knocked his head against the wall. In the cell he was most noisy and violent, and damaged the closet. In order to quieten him another Pole was placed with him. For assaulting the police, the prisoner was sentenced to 28 days' hard labour with- out the option of a fine and for the drunkenness he was fined ss. and costs.
AtrzumN Snow next Tuesday and Wednesday.—J. and W. DuTToN, Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt. A HALTON FARMER'S TROUBLESOME VISITORS. _

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Richard Williams and Thomas Grindley were charged in custody with doing damage to a field of oats to the value of 6d.—William Parry, Flighfield Farm, Halton, stated that on Sunday morning, between five and six o'clock, he went into the hay-loft, and his suspicions were aroused that someone was sleeping there by seeing men's clothes hanging on the beams. He sent for a police con- stable, but on his arrival the prisoners had gone. Ho, however, saw them running across a field of oats, and gave chase. They were arrested, and subsecpently locked up. Mr. tarry said he had .been very much troubled with tramps about his place, and only recently he had a fire at his farm.—The prisoners were each ordered to pay ss. and costs, or go to gaol for seven days. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT HALTON PARISR CHURCH. . .
The harvest festival in connection with St. Mary's Church, Halton, took place on Friday, when Holy Com- munion was celebrated at 8.15 in the morning. In the

evening a sermon was preached by the Rev. Clement Bird, M.A., Minor Canon of Chester Cathedral. There was very good congregation, and the sacred edifice was tastefully decorated with all kinds of pr^ducts of the season by friends and members of the congregation. On Sunday the thanksgiving services were continued when a sermon was preached by the Vicar,preceded by prayer and Holy Communion (choral). In the afternoon, at three o'clock, a children's service was held, and at the evening service the sermon was preached by the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, M.A., vicar of Runcorn, and rural dean of Frodsham. All the services on Sunday were also well attended. The collections on Friday were for church expenses, and on Sunday at the morning and evening services, for the Halton-road Mission-room, and at the children's service for the Universities Mission to Central Africa.

COWARDLY ATTACK ON A WIDNIS WOMAN. Patrick Devereaux, cf Victoria-st.,was brought before the Widnes magistrates on Monday, to answer a charge of wounding Mrs. Mayne, of Ann-st., by stabbing her on the face, in conjunction with another woman named Sarah Walker. Mrs. Mayne keeps a refreshment shop in Ann-st., and on Saturday night the prisoner and another young man entezed and ordered potato pie. After they had eaten the pie, the prisoner demanded his money back, and Mrs. Mayne told him to go home. At once the prisoner struck her on the 'cheek and blood flowed freely from a wound caused by the blow. Dr. O'Keeffe informed the Bench that the woman suffered from a punctured wound under the left eye about half an inch long, and penetrating to the bone.—The prisoner said he did not stab the woman but knocked her down.—Dr. O'Keeffe replied that the wound could not have been caused by a fall or there would have been other marks on the face. As the woman was very weak from loss of blood and unable to appear in court, the prisoner was remanded for a week. THE REV A. SANDERSON OF RUNCORN.

This gentleman has again been the recipient of presents from those whom he is about to leave. The members of Trinity l Band °Mope have presented him with a silver pencil case and penholder and the choir have given him a silver-mounted walking stick.

RUNCORN SCIENOE AND ART CLASSES. These classes commence at the Board School, Greenwity-road on Monday evening. Full particu- lars may be obtained from Mr. Moss. the clerk. RUNCORN. T.D.:1,1C SAL-FA CONCERT,' The first concert of the season will be given on Monday evening in the Public Hall. Well known and competent artistes have been engaged and a 'high class concert may be anticipated. RaVISION OF VCTEIIB LISTS AT RUNCORN. The annual revision of the list of voters of the .Northwich Parliamentary Division has been held during; the past week by Mr. C. E. Lloyd. On Thursday he visitedV.uncorn, but nothing of special interest transpired. Mr. W. Handley represented the Liberals, and Mr.. C. J. Hughes the Conserva- tives,.

RESULT OF Tffa ST. HELENS REVISION". Mr. ..I. Bain, the Liberal agent, has issued the ollowing :.—Liberal claims allowed, 126; Conserv- ptive claims allowed, 70; Liberal gain on claims, 56i Conservatives struck off on objection. 356; Liberals struck off, on objections, 34; Liberal gain on objections, .10. Total Liberal gain on revision, 66. BASSINETTES.—J. S. Garland, Ironinonwkr, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington.— Advt. A TRAMP'S DODGE.

The Ilaydock -police arrested a tramp named John Renshaw for drunkenness, and when on Monday they started for Warrington to put him before the magistrates, he suddenly became helpless,and none of the efforts of the officers could induce him to move. Under these circumstances, the charge being only one of drunkenness, a magisterial discharge was obtained. As soon as John heard the good news he jumped to his feet, and, laughing at his success— ful ruse, made off as fast as he could go. AUTUMN Slio-fr next Tuesday and Weduesday.—J. and W. Durrox, Sankey-st., Warrington.—.Add.

ing of ratepayers, and they had unanimously passed a resolution asking the Authority,before proceeding with, this scheme to have a water district formed includiag portion of the Township and Lerdship,which were equaily in want,of water.—Mr. Lewis,: -What has the Township. to do with a portion of the Lerdship ? I shall:move that the Township mind their own business, and let the Lordship mind their own.—Mr. Edwards : That is really what we.want you to do, but:this scheme has been thriist upon the Township by the -Lordship. (No, so.) Mr. Edwardsswent on to argue that as a matter of • CalittialCll fairness and justice a water-district should, be. formed. He again characterised the p,resent scheme as . wild and incompreliensive, and said there was a plentiful sucoly of water on the high land. without pumping it up-from the bed of the river almost, The ratepayers were sitnply disgusted with the - scheme.—Mr. Reynelds : Question.—Mr. Edwards:: Then the maj9rity a the ratepayers.—Mr. Reynolds.:. Ns,. I won't aglee to that,—Mr. Edwards:: Ii am prepared to have a poll 4 taken.—He went on Aro state that the scheme wculd cost 26,000 or £7,000, and the rates. which. were Bow 35... ad. would, if this scheme were carried out, jump up to I's 2d in the 2, and although paying such heavy rates they had none of the advantages of a town. He must persevere in his resolution to have the minute rescinded and.referred back for, further consideration.—M-4 Aaron said he thought it a great. hardship that the pneceedings of.a.committee to which,the authority. had delegated its powers should be attempted to be sqyashed in this manner. The Local Government Board would send down an inspector to investigate--the whole of the plans, and if Mr. Edwards could show, to him that it was a wild selieme,.then there would be an end of it.. It was a waste of time bringing. the matter, forward meeting after meeting. —ln reply to Mr. Reynolds, the-clerk, said after this scheme was carried out a water district could be formed. It was a qpestion for the two parishes. The scheme would do jpst as well for a district of the two parishes as it would for the township, He had written to the Local Government Board asking if they would sanction the formation of a district if the Authority thought fit to form, one. He-had not received a reply. Some years ago Mr. Linaker made the samoinquiry and they would not sanction it then. The Local Govern- ment Board seemed rather averse to forming these small districts.—Mr. Reynolds: The expense. is so great.— Mr. W. Whitlow, said this was a very serious item and required great consideration. He seconded Mr. Edwards's motion.—The Clerk:. The Committee will say if that were passed "we may as well dissolve."—Mr. Reynolds: That is, what it will come to.—Mr. Aaron moved a resolution supporting the minutes.—Mr. Reynolds seconded, and remarked that a few years ago it was proved before a Government Inspector that the Lordship did not require water works. A Government Inspector would decide the present scheme, and Mr. Edwards would have ample opportunity of showing to that gentleman that the scheme wat what he stated it to be. He himself considered it a cheap and feasible scheme, and his opinion was•equally weighty with that of Mr. 'Edwards wh• was neither a water nor a civil engineer.—The motion on being put was declared lost by five votes to three.—Mr. Edwards challenged the counting, and a second vote was taken with the result that his motion was carried by five votes to four. There voted for: Messrs. Knowles, Whitlow,J.Baguley,Stokes, and Edwards; against : Messrs. Reynolds,Aarob, Lewis, and Priestner.—lt was pointed out to the Chairman that he had not voted on the second occasion, and ho remarked that the motion practically referred the scheme back fel- further consideration,aud they were better able to deal with it than he was.

div.p: TIIE STIPBNDIAILY QUESTION AT ST. HELENS.

A meeting of the Parliamentary Committee was held on Wednesday, when the question of blie proposed stipendiary and quarter sessions for he borough was under consideration. The committee adopted a resolution declaring that it was inexpedient at the present time to take any steps with the view of securing the appointment of a stipendiary magistrate. The matter- of a quarter sessions for the borough was left over for consideration at the next meeting of the con:mitten. AUTUMN SHOW next Tuesday and Wednesday.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. THE DOCKERS' CONFERENCE.

The whole of Thursday's proceedings of the Dockers' Conference at Hull were conducted in private. At the close of the proceedings Mr. Ben Tillett informed the representatives bf the Press that it had been resolved to consider at their next meet-

ing proposals which had been made for amalgamation with the Middlesbrough Stevedores' Union, the St. Helens Chemical Workers' Union, and the National Labour Federation of Newcastle. The delegates were afterwards entertained by the Mayor.

div.head: RIGHT MOVE AT DUTTON.
div.p: A RIGHT MOVE AT DUTTON.

In 1887 the master of the Dutton Board School (with the approval of the members) started a penny bank in connection with the Post Office. Since that time over .£l3O has been deposited and placed to the credit of the chileren attending the school. As the members of the Board have decided to make all fees, books, Bz.c., free from the 28th inst., they particularly wish to impress upon parents and scholars the desitability of placing to the credit of their children the fees which they have previously paid. It may be added that married women can also deposit in this bank, the Government paying 24 per cent. per annum interest.
Tom MANN IN A WESLEYAN _PULPIT

Mr. Tom Mann, of London, the well-known trade ; unionist,who was the principal speaker at the trades demonstration at St. Helens on Saturday afternoon, preached in the Nutgrove Wesleyan Chapel, St. Helens, on Sunday night. In the course of his sermon, Mr. Marti alluded to his former active con- nection with religious efforts, and said he felt called to come out in the labour movement and help in the solution of the great problems affecting the trades of the country. He urged that as real Christians they were bound to work for the elevation of the masses—morally, socially, physically, and spiritu- ally. It was a duty of the Christian Church to de- clare war against many of the conditions of life and labour which existed at the present day. Hitherto the Church had only assisted the labour movement sectionally, but the assistance should be universal, and the Church should throw its whole heart and soul into the work. Religion and labour,he said,were inseparable,and because a man was a trades unionist it did not follow that he was irreligious. fie exhorted his hearers to be just in all their dealings, and expressed a hope that in striving to. att.ain to a higher conception of life they would assist in a true solution of the great labour problem of the day. THE VYRNWY WATER SUPPLY AND THE WORK AT FIDLER'S FERRY.

At a meeting of the Vyrnwy Works Sub-Com- mittee of the Liverpool Water Committee held on Tuesday afternoon at the Municipal-buildings, Liverpool, it was stated that the works at Fidler's Ferry in connection with the permanent pipe-line from Vyrnwy had been stopped owing to some de- rangement of the boring machinery in connection with the " shield." It was thought, however, that the delay would not be of great duration, and that before long the work would be resumed. The following weekly report from Mr. Deacon appeared in the epitome of the proceedings of Committees which was published on Tuesday :—" The face of the shield when work ceased on Saturday was 170 feet six inches from the centre of the shaft, being an advance of eight feet nine inches during the week. I have reason to hope that the contractors will before long modify the method of driving, much to the advantage of the work." It was resolved by the Committee to write to the contractors for the Man- chester Ship Canal works, urging them to get that portion of the canal which is to be crossed by the permanent line of pipes finished as quickly as possible. A prolonged discussion afterwards took place as to the details of the scheme, but no definite resolution was arrived at upon any point. atEa LAwNrlestown. div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Mr. Mclntyre presided, and there were present Messrs. C. Reynolds, J. P. Knowles. Aaron, Lewis. W. Whitlow, J. Edwards, Baguley, J. Stokes, J. W. Kirkham, P. Hall, G. Prif;stner, J. Aston (clerk).
WIDNES GASES AND VEGETATION.

The Clerk said in reply to the complant of the damage caused to vegetation in the Union by gases from Widnes, Mr. E. Carey, secretary to the United Alkali Company, asked him to make known to the Authority that since the various works were taken over by the Company there had been less escape of gas than ever previously; also that the greatest care was being and would continue to be taken to prevent escapes.—Mr. W. Whitlow said the escape of gases had been greater since the Alkali Union took the works and Mr. C. Reynolds was of the same opinion.—Mr. Whitlow said on two or three occasions this year he had never seen so much dam- age done in so short a time.—The Clerk said nothing further could be done except by drawing the attention of the Government Inspector to the matter.—Mr. W. Wkitlow : I fancy he goes on his holidays very often. (Laughter.) Mr. Aaron said the process which was the principal cause of the nuisance from Widnes was worked at Mr. Chance's place at Birmingham without the slight- est nuisance arising, and it the plant were properly con- structed at Widnes and ordinary care exercised in work- ing it there would not he this escape of noxious vapours. The discussion then ceased. THE PLANS OF SEWERS. The Clerk said he had gone through the plans of sewers in his possession, and they were far from com- plete.—Mr. Aaron said at Weston some years ago £3OO or £4OO were spent on works of sewerage, and plans were drawn by Mr. C. Linaker,which the Authority paid for.—The Clerk said those plans had not come into his possession.—Mr. Lewis: Have you asked for them from Mr. Linaker's office ?—The Clerk: No, I have not asked for them; they are supposed to have handed everything over to this Authority. If I were to ask for anything I should take the authority of the Board.—Mr. Aaron proposed that the Clerk ask for the plans of the new sewers at Weston, and for any other plans belonging to the Authority.—Mr. Aaron strongly urged that Mr. Wells,the engineer, should be engaged to indicate" the whole 6of the sewers of the Union on the Ordnance Map, but the Clerk said he had spoken to Mr. Farrington, the nuisance inspector, who said he could do the work.—The motion was carried. div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. J. Mclntyre presided, and there were present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. J. Knowles, S. Taylor, Aaron, Lewis, Stokes,, Kirkham, P. Hall, T. Lea, G. Prestner, J. Baguley, W. Whitlow, Baxter, Edwards, Brandreth, J. Ashton, (clerk )—The Clerk read a letter from Mr. G. Howard, enquiry office,. Runcorn., stating he had received several. applications for school fees and asking if he should call the committee of Gualdians together for the purpose of granting fees.—The, Olerk said where children attendad a school which was,not free the Guardians might pay fees. Where children attended a free school the duty of Guardians at once ceased in respeet to these children.. If parents desired to. send their children to the Wesleyan school or the iiiburch school which are not free,. the parent could no be compelled to send them,to a free school, and if necessary the Guardians must pay the fees. The Guardians: need not now be lavish in granting fees, —Mr. Taylor said this was very important inform- ation.

THE CASUALS.--AN EXTENSION REQUIRED. On the Ist September the Government Inspector made the following entry in the Visitors Book:—" The vagrant wards have been frequently overcrowded, and it will be necessary for the Guardians. to provide further accom- modation for male vagrants." in consequence the , master was instructed to obtain information from other I Unions and report.—The Master reported that the ac- commodation at the House consisted of seven cells for males and two double cells for females and the cells are frequently overcrowded. He had carefully considered how further provision could be made for vagrants at the House, and if cells are to be provided for sleeping- and stone-breaking the land near the stables would be the best available site. This, however, would entail a considerable , outlay for new buildings, and as an alternative he would suggest that an association ward fitted with Woods's patent mattresses be provided for 10 or 12 casuals, ad- joining the present casual ward, when the present system of heating could be extended rand at the same time light- and ventilation of some of the oh l cells might be im- proved, and it would be a suitable opportunity for re- plaoing the present wooden slopes with the wire mat- tresses as the Local Government Iloard have already con- demned the plank beds throughout the country. On the ' 2reiT,SitiQn gf tile Roy. J, W. N. Tanner, the following genllemen were ton.siituied a committee to deal with the matter :—Messrs. Aaron, Kirkham, Stokes, Taylor, Brandreth, Lea, Edwara;, Baxter, and Tanner.

DEATH OF TEE REV. 0. P. WRALLEY.

Much regret will be felt in Warrington at the death of the Rev. 0. P. Whalley, principal of the Ripon Training College,and formerly lecturer at the Warrington Training College, which took place at the residence of his father,Gaywood Rectory,King's. Lynn, on Satttrday. On Christmas Eve, Mr. Whal- ley, while returning from Ripon, after his appoint- ment, caught a cold, and was ill during the greater part of the Christmas holidays. He returned to Warrington on January 27th, to get ready to go to Ripon on January 10th, but had an attack of con- gestion of the lungs, confining him to his room for several weeks. He commenced his duties at Ripon on April 4th. On June 20th, an interesting present- ation was made to him at the Warrington Training College. It took the form of a Queen Anne after- noon tea service in electro-plate, six afternoon tea- spoons and sugar tongs in silver, two china teacups and saucers, and an oak and ebony tray. The tea- pot bore the following inscription :—" Presented to the Rev. Oswald P. Whalley, by the teachers and students of the Warrington Training College, 1888- 1890. June 20, 1891." The "Training College Magazine "of February, 1891, contained the follow- ing:—" The students of 1888-1890, will not easily forget the Lecturer, whose genial manner, kind heart, readiness to help, overflowing manner, and true manliness endeared him to all. The teachers will ever remember him. He came to us fresh from Oxford, and at once fell into our ways,helped when- ever he could, and was soon as much in harmony as if he had worked with us for years. THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIGNS.

It nowseems more than probable that there will be contests at the coming municipal elections in all, or nearly all, of the nine wards into whicl3 Warrington is divided. It is true that, as yet, it cannot be said that many opposing candidates are in the field, but it is c.ertain that both political parti,3s appear disposed to take up a helligerent attitude towards each other. The retiring candi- dates are, as we mentioned a week or two ago, as follows :

Town 'Hall Ward, Mr. INPierpoint. Whitecross, Mr. Plumpton. Btwsey, Mr. Flood. at. John's, Mr. Garnar,. Orford, Mr. Jenkins. Itirfield, Mr. Hutchinson. Howley, Mr. Bolton. St. Austin's Mr. Voisey.. Latchford, ?Mr. J, Fairclough. It will be seen, therefore, that four of the retiring ;20uncillors are Liberals,and five Conservatives. It is understood that alltof-them,with the possible excep- tion of Mr. Voisey, are likely to again ask for the 'suffrages of the ratepayecs. Mr. Voisey, it is stated is not inclined to ootne forward owing to business engagements. For the vacancy that will thus be caused in St. Austin's Ward, the Liberals have already set about obtaining a candidate. The Liberal Ward Committee at a recent meeting unan- imously decided to invite Mrlailiaa Winser to cham- pion their cause. Mr. Winser has mot yet announced his decision,but it is anticipated, that he will accede to the request that has been conveyed to him. It is scarcely necessary to say that be will make an excellent candidate;: and, apart altogether from any question of politics, he would, if elected,"be a decided acquisition to the TOwn Council. The Con -. servatives have, in recent elections, retained their hold of St. Austin's Ward by slender majorities, that at the last election being only 11, and with a can- didat such as Mr. Winser would be the chances of the Liberals wresting the seats from their opponents are very favourable. Notwithstanding their two heavy defeats within twelve mcnths, the Conserva- tives still seem disposed to contest Whitecross Ward against Mr. Plumpton. Mr. A. Woods, who was probably as strong a candidate as they could put in the field, does not seem disposed to court a third defeat, and his place is now understood to be taken by Mr. W. Bellian, who is described as a working- man. It is not expected that Mr. Plumpton will find much difficulty in giving a satisfactory account of this new opponent. The Warrington Trades and Labour Council originally intended to bring labour candidates out of both Howley and Latchford Wards, and, as we have before mentioned, Mr. T. Malkin, secretary for the Warrington branch of the Associated Ironworkers, has been selected to contest Howley ward against ' Councillor Bolton. At a special meeting of the Council, held on Tuesday evening, it was decided, ' after an animated discussion, to contest Howley Ward only.
THE MAY ORA.LTY OF WARRINGTON.

Although. the 9th of November, the date on which towns like Warrington elect their first magistrate, is rapidly approaching, there seems to be remark- ably little speculation as to who the next Mayor is to be. Alderman Francomb has now held the office close upon two years, and it will be remembered that twelve months ago he was quite prepared to hand over the honours and responsibilities of the position to a successorg a willing and suitable one could have been found. But upon that score some difficulties were encountered. Mr. F. Monks, Mr. R Davies,Alderman Platt,and Councillor Voisey were all invited to allow themselves to be elected, but all declined, and, in fact, the Mayoralty went " a-begging," as the phrase is. It is probable , that this year nothing will be done towards selecting the Mayor till after the elections on the first of November. For a considerable number of years now the Conservative have had an uneisputed majority in the Town Council, and have therefore, had the disposal of the Mayoralty pretty much in their own hands. It is, however, quite within the range of probability that at the corning elections this majority may be turned into a minority. Con- sequently, until the relative positions of the two. parties have been determined it is not likely 'nat any decided steps towards the "selection 4 V OP Mayor will 1.)0
THE RECENT ATTEMPTED SITICIDIL
APPLICATION FOR MAINTENANCE.

At the Warrington borough police court, yester- day. Mr. P. Davies, solicitor, said he was appearing that morning for a man, Thomas Worsley, puddler, of Haydock-street, who was brought up on Thurs- day week, on a charge of attempting suicide. Their worships would recollect that Dr. Adams gave evid- ence that it was a most marvellous thing that the man had come round ; and that the Chief-Constable gave him a most excellent character. The case was disposed of by his being discharged and bound over in his own recognizances and these of his sons tor his future good behaviour. The attempt upon his life had been brought about through his being driven to despera- tion by a drunken wife. He was still under the doctor and quite unfit to do work. The case was hardly cold before the woman had the audacity to come to the magistrates' office and ask them to send her husband to prison if he did not allow her some- thing for maintenance. Dr. Adams in court had stated that the woman must be kept away from him or he would never get better. She had behaved in a mcst abominable manner, and since the trial had not been sober a single night. He (Mr. Davies) considered the woman oughtto be left to seek herremedy from the Guardians, though he did not think they would be likely to come down upon her husband under the cir- cumstances.—Mrs. Worsley, who had taken out a sum- mons against her husband charging him with desertien, was called. She admitted she was prohibited by Dr. Adams from coining to the house. She had been to the house since the trial. She did not tell her husband that he had not ent his throat deep enough. She had never been drunk at all.—Mr. Davies said he had evidenc., toprove that both these latter statements were untrue. He ap- plied that the case might be adjourned a mouth, or that she might be left to apply to the Guardians. Her hus- band was perfectly willing to allow her maintenance at a future date. The case was adjourned for a month.

div.head: LECTURE 13Y THE REV. C. P. AREA
div.p: LECTURE 13Y THE REV. C. P. AREA

The autumn session of Brunswick Mutual Improvement Class, Runcorn, was opened on Tit urs- day evening, in Brunswick School by a lecture on "Marcus Aurelius and his times, or the early days of Christianity." The lecturer was the Rev. C. F. Aked, of Pembroke Chapel, Liverpool, who gave a vivid and thrilling description of the state of society of the heathen in the days of Marcus Aurelius, who reigned in the second century, and from the stirring , events of that time be drew practical lessons for the present day. lie quoted from Gibbon and other ' great authors, and his lecture throughout gave evidence of great research, and wide reading on his part. Gibbon, he said, gave five reasons for the spread and progress of Christianity. and two of , these were the pure lives of the early Christians and the zeal and enthusiasm with which they propag- ated their faith. At the present time all attempts at enthusiasm and zeal were frowned down, but he wished them to emulate the early Christians and success was certain to result. For upwards of an hour Mr. Aked kept his crowded audience enthralled by the spell of his eloquence,which was distinguished.by a fervour and oratorical method seldom met with. The meeting was a good augury for the success of the session.—On the motion of the Rev. W. Arrowsmith seconded by Mr. J. D. Jones,a vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer and a similar compliment was paid to the chairman on the motion of the lecturer seconded by Mr. W. Millington. Mr. T. Simister, the president of the class occupied the chair.

div.head: BLACK BISHOP AT RUNCORN.
div.p: A BLACK BISHOP AT RUNCORN.

Under the auspices of the Runcorn Primitive Methodist Chapel, Bishop Hawkins, of the Episco- palian Methodist Church. Canada, delivered a lecture on "My slave life and how I escaped from it." Mr. Y. Speakman. C.C., presided, and there was a good attendance. The choir occupied a gallery behind the platform, and sang several hymns dur- ing the evening. In opening the proceedings, the Chairman said it rave him great pleasure to preside over that meeting. He had through life taken a deep interest in missionary work, and it gave him the greatest pos- sible pleasure to find a good old veteran missionary on the platform. (Applause.) One who had lived the life of a slave and was now living and had lived for a great number of years the life of a Christian, and who had come to enlist their sympathy in his work and in the work of their Common Master. After referring to the great fight there was to have slavery abolished, Mr. Speakman said it was his good fortune to be in Palestine this year and he had seen that memorable spot where our Saviour laid his head low that we might be saved and he should never forget the moment when at the dawn of day, he saw the grave of our Lord, and stood where Mary stood when she saw her Saviour had gone away. This grave was where the foundation stone of Christianity was laid and he believed that foundation would grew more firm and their prosperity increase un- til they were all gathered to Christ himself. (Applause.) Bishop Hawkins then proceeded to deliver his lecture. Although 83years of age, the bishop is straight and up- right as a young man, and he possesses a physical vigour seldom found when the allotted span has been passed. for two hours he spoke with a power and eloquence that maintained the interest of the audieece in his narrative until the conclusion. He described the inhuman cruelties practiced to the black man in his early days, and said the laws of the country made it a crime to be black. His escape from slavery to the protection of the British flag on Canadian territory, was pourtrayed in language that enabled the audience to realise vividly the dangers and privations he had to undergo. His remrrks were inter- spersed with numerous humorous comments upon men and things, and these never failed to produce much merriment in the auditory. in the course of the even- ing Bishop Hawkins sang several characteristic negro hymns.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY. CONVERSAZIONE AT THE MUSEUM.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY. CONVERSAZIONE AT THE MUSEUM.

A very successful conversazione was held in the Art Gallery and Museum, on Thursday evening, in connection with the Warrington Musical Society. There was a large attendance, about 300 persons being present. The entrance and stairs to the Art Gallery was laid with carpet, and, inside, some tasteful decorations had been carried out by Messrs. R. Garnett and Sons. Plants and flowers, sent by various members of the Society, were dispersed throughout the rooms and gave a pleasing freshness to the scene. The attractions of the display were further heightened by the many and various-coloured fairy lamps,—lent by Mrs. Pearson—which were placed in suitable places. In addition to the above, the usual contents of the Museum and Art Gallery were open to the inspection of those present, and it may be mentioned, that at the present time there are some particularly interesting objects on view. Conspicuous amongst these is a 'case contain- ing the curios, collected in Abyssinia, the Soudan, and Cyprus, lent by Major Mackie. This very in- teresting collection includes a fragment of a diary kept at Khartoum, during the siege in 1884, by Col. Stewart of the 11th qussars. It may be remembered that Col. Stewart was, during the siege of Khartoum by the Mandi, despatched down the Nile by Gordon to confer with General Wolseley, who was in com- mand of the relief expedition. Ile was accom- panied by a considerable number of other persons, ' but in the passage down the river the boat was wrecked near a village named llebbeh, and the whole of the party were slaughtered by the Mah- dists. The particular fragment of the diary now in the Museum was afterwards picked up by Major Mackie himself in the hut in which the unfor.tunate Colonel Stewart was murdered. In addition to the above, Major Mackie's loan includes several wea- pons of war from Abyssinia and the Soudan, a medal struck by Gordon at Khartoum, lamps from Egyptian tombs, specimens of Cypriole embroidery, &c. There is also to be seen at the Museum just now, a Whitworth measuring machine,an ingenious piece of mechanism ,capable of measuring to the

40.000t1 part of an • inch. All these obj ects,, besides the many others ta be seen in the Museum, and Art Gallery,were viewed with interest by thosepresent at the conversazione. It should be added that suit- able refreshments which had been provided by the Ladies' Committee of the Society, were dispensed during the evening in the large Lecture Rocm. Au excellent programme of music had been ar- ranged,and was rendered by members of the•society. It included pianctorte solos, "Norwegian,Dance," and" March of the mountain gnomes' by. Miss M. Chandley ; and the following songs," In the Chim- ney Corner," by Miss'Cavanagh ; " Lightin dark- ness." Mrs. Pearson "Come into the garden Maud," Mr. 'VV . S. Howard; " Ernani, involami," Miss Newcombe ;" In old Madrid," Miss Fanshawe; and" Hybrias the Cretan," by Mr. R. ncles. All of these pieces were rendered in a meritorious fashion, Miss Nawcombe and Mr. Eccles, in particu- lar, receiving oordial encores. The three Massa Brothers—two violins and a harp—also rendered, in a way which won general admiration, a selection of light music. The conversazione, which was a very enjoyable one, terminated about half-past ten.

SUDDEN DEATH OF A CHILD AT GRAPPENITALt: Hannah Hatton, aged seven months, daughter of John flatton, residing in Knutsford-road, Grappen— hall, died suddenly on Sunday morning. The child had been ill since birth, and had been attend by a doctor until two months ago. Early on Sunday morning it suddenly grew worse, and died a few minutes afterwards. No inquest was considered necessary.
CROFT HORTICULTURAL SOCIRTY.

The annual prize distribution in connection with the above society took place in the Board School, on Saturday evening, when the members, their wives, and friends sat down to an excellent tea. After tea the chair was taken by Mr. Cawthorne, the new-appointed headmaster, who also distributed. the prizes. The prizes amounted to .£l6 12s. 6d. A hearty vote of thanks w 4 given to the Committee, officers, and to Mr. J. Winston for the excellent tea he had provided. We understand that, after paying all expenses, there will remain a balance in hand. A_ REFRACTORY RAILWAY PASSENGER.

At NVarrington occasional Court, on Monday morning, before Mr. W. IL Bleckley, John Prescot was charged with being drunk at Glazebrook Station on the 19th September. Mr. Percy Davies prosecuted on behalf of the Cheshire Lines Commit.. tee. He stated that the prisoner was asleep in a second-class compartment at Glazebrook, and on being awakened by the stationmaster, asked what station he was at. On being told and asked for his ticket, he produced one from Bickershaw to Abram. On the stationaaaster telling him he had over- travelled his ticket he refused to pay the difference in fare. He created a disturbance, and an officer was sent for and he was given in charge. The stationmaster and a porter corroborated this state- ment, and prisoner was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. AUTUMN SILOW next Tuesday and Wednesday.—J. and W. DUTTON, San key-st.. Warrington. —Aevt. THE SUPPORT OF A. MOTHER.

On Monday, at the Bolton County Police Court, William Harter, of Warrington, was summoned for neglecting to support his mother.—Mr. Churnside, a relieving officer, to the Bolton Union, stated that the case was before the Court a month ago, the de- fendant having promised to keep his mother, but he had been unable to see her. There were three sons, who paid 2s. per week each,but the defendant had not contributed anything towards the support of his mother for some time.—Defendant said he , was willing and able to keep his mother, and would provide her a home, and he could do no more. His mother kept going from daughter to daughter, and she would be much better living with him.—Ann Harter, the mother, who said she was over 70 years of age, was called, and stated that she preferred to live with her daughter, and did not care to live away from Bolton. Her son Henry thought she had some money, but she had none, as it was made away with by her late husbwd.—Defendant said his mother had money. If he sent her money she never received it. He did not wish an order. to be made, as he would pay.—The Bench pointed out that the defendant had failed to pay anything to his mother since the case was adjourned, and made an order for 29. per Week.—Defendant: As long as I offer her a home I shall not pay.

Eliza Smith, 51s appearance, for indecent conduet in Scotland-road, the previous night was sentenced to a month's imprisonment with hard labour.—Elizabeth Goodfellow was charged with like conductin Arpley-road at 12.50 a.m. the same day. On being apprehended she threw herself down and commenced kicking, and it took two constables to take her to the station.—She was dis- charged on promising to leave the town immediately.

div.head: .TEZET OF BOOTS.
div.p: .TEZET OF BOOTS.

-ioseph Frederick Burke, Ship Canal' labourer, was charged with stealing, the previous 'evening, from the shop of Frederick Jenkins,l94, Bridge-st., a pair of men's boots.—P.C. 38 deposed to seeing the man with the boots with no wrapper on them. He stopped him and asked him where he got them, and he replied that he had paid es. ed. for them. Witness gOt hold of him, and hethrew the boots behindhim, and tried to get away, but with the assistance of another constable witness brought him to the police station.—The prisoner now stated that he was drunk at the time, and he bought the boots from a man he did not know.—Mr. Jenkins, who was not sworn, identified as his, some boots proddced taken from the prisoncr.—He was sent tujail for 14 days' hard labour.

'TIM FIRE IN BRIDGE-ST.—IMPROVING TIIE OCCASION. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, yesterday, George Holden, a young man, was charged with steal- ing, on Thursday night, one lady's cloth jacket and a lady's velvet tippet, the property of Madame Lilley, milliner, 128, Bridge.st. The prisoner pleaded not guilty.—A P.C. said there was a fire on Madame Lilley's premises, and he was on duty in plain Clothes in Bridge-st. There were a large number of people there, and a lot of suspicions characters and cornermen about. He saw the prison9r come from the crowd to- wards Bridge-foot, with something bulky under his jacket. Witness found that he had the articles men- tioned, and that they had been damaged by the fire. They were now wortk fis., but had been worth £4 4s.— Elizabeth Wright identified, the articles as the complain- ant's.—luspector Spinks said the prisoner was 200 yards from the fire when the constable stopped him.—The prisoner said he picked the things up after the fire, and did not steal them. He had never stolen anything in his life.—The Chairman (Mr. Garnett) said the Bench were disposed to give him the benefit of the doubt, but were satisfied that he had taken the things and concealed them with the intention of keeping them. • Be would be fined 10s., including costs, in default 7 days.

div.head: THEFTS BY A LODGING-HOUSE SERVANT.
div.p: THEFTS BY A LODGING-HOUSE SERVANT.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Wednes- day, Bridget McEvoy, wife of John McEvoy, of No. 9, Ship Yard, was charged with stealing from the lodging- house of Alfred Bruchemite, Friars Green, some time between the Ist and the 21st inst., two blankets, one sheet, three towels, one pillow case, one hand basin, and a bass, value 10s. in all. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the prosecution. He stated that the prisoner had been en- gaged for about three months past in helping the prosec- tor at his lodging-house, and she had been provided by him with a key which fitted the door of every room in the house.—Mr. Bruchemite said the prisoner had been acting as washerwoman and charwoman for him and lived close to his lodging-house. In ,consequence of missing certain things from there he; Detective- Sergeant Monaghan, and Inspector Bowen went on Tuesday to her house. She denied having anything there that did not belong to her, but the articles as to which she was charged, together with a curtain missed by him, were found ia the house. She said she had had the things since she came to England.—Mrs. Clegg who had been lodging at the prisoner's house had seen one of the blankets produced on her bed and another on Mc- Evoy's husband's. The prisoner said she had brought them from Ireland,and had another in pawn.—Elizabeth Bruchemire, the prosecutor's wife,identified the articles. Sergeant Monaghan and Inspector Bowen also gave evi- dence Monoghan stating that the prisoner first asserted she had brought the things from Ireland and then that Mrs. Bruchemire had given her them.—She now repeated the latter statement lier sister, Winifred Hennessy, said six weeks ag , , tol,l her this.—The pri- soner was senter t, 4 days imprisonment, but later on, on the inter( ,f her si:-'•er, who said her child would die if his CVA Lab away, the sentence was altered to a " arid )Sts.
