div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH poLroP, COURT. SATuttnAy.,-Before Alderman Burgess (in the chair), Councillor Voisey, and Mr. John Geddes. . DiatanK IN THE PARK.—Catherine Riley, who said she was tramping to Manchester, was charged with being drunk in Bank Park on Friday afternoon.—The park keeper said that on the date named, at half-past two, his attention was called to a ivoman being asleep in one of le buildings. On going there he found the woman

asleep, and awakened her. She refused to leave the place, and became•very violent. A eonstable was sent • for, and she was locked up.—Fined ss. and costs. A DESERTER.—Gearge Dyson was charged with being a diserter from the Rifle Brigade, stationed at Win- chester, since the 31st July, 1839.—11 e was remanded to Strangeways goal to await the arrival of an escort. MONDAY.—Before the yayor (Alderman. R. W, Fran- comb, anti Alderman Sutton. DRUNIC AND DISORDERLY.—James Scurry,in Whittle-st. on Saturday afternoon, 23. 6d. and cests.—Joseph Skin- ner, in Sankey-st. on Saturday night. He was having apparent fits and asking for brandy, but on being taken to Dr. Spinks he said he was shamming to get brandy. 10s. and costs.—Rosanna Finley, in Naylor-st., on Satur- day night, 10s. and costs or seven days.—Andrew Cane was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Mersey- st. at 1.50 p.m. on Sunday, also with being in posses- sion of a pair of boots supposed to have been stolen.— The prisoner said the boots had been given to him by a gentleman in Earlestown.—Ald. Sutton thought they were too new for that.--th prisoner was fined 10s. or 7 days' hard labour.—Samuel Jackson. was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Haydock-st., on the 12th, and William Hardman, with being disorderly. He was stripped to the waist and challenging Jackson to fight. Hardman said he was challenging a man named Flan- naghan, who came to his house annoying him, not Jack- son. Jackson fined ss. and Hardman bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months. William Jones. drunk and disorderly in Winwick-st., on the 12th inst., 10s., or seven days' hard labour. FIGHTING.—Henry Taylor and John Mullin, were charged with fighting in Pitt-st., on the sth inst. Mullin did not appear and a warrant was ordered for him to pay costs 7s. 6d., Taylor was bound over to keeP the peace for six months.—Thomas Droy and Enoch Alien, puddlers, were charged with fighting in Pitt-st. on the sth instl—The Mayor remarked that he,should have thought they had exercise enough as puddlers without ' fighting. To nay the costs 7s. each, and bound over ' for six months.—John Mullin, for whom a warrant had been ordered, on a charge of fighting now made his appearance. He and Thomas Mullin were charged with fighting in Pitt-st.. on the 29th of August. The Chief Constable said he was unable to prove the charge against Thomas and would withdraw it. There was no moral doubt they were fighting, and there was such disorderly conduct going on in that neighbourhood that it would be serious for somebody if it was not discontinued.—Thomas was dismissed; John was also discharged.—William and Peter Quinn, bro- thers, fighting in Rylands-yard, on the 11th inst. They had to pay ss. and costs each, and were bound over to keep the peace.—Peter Higgins and James Rooney, for fighting in Ship Yard on Sunday night.—The Mayor: I see, Rooney, you have a good character from the army. They want fighting men in the army. Did you ever get in a dust? Were you in Egypt ?=Rconey : Yes, I was, but I didn't get to the front.—Tne Mayor: It is very well you were not there. There would have been sOmething .dotte. You got on very well with the officers of the army but you didn't get on very well with the officers in War- rington. Higgins was bound over,and Rooney was fined ss. costs.—Patric lc Dooley and John McDonnell, for fighting in Rylands Street, on the 15th inst., were bound over for 6 months, and ordered to pay costs. TIIESDA.Y.—Before Mr. E. J. Guest (chairman) and Capt.

_ Ridgway. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—TWO FAMILIAR BEAUTIES. —Bodelia Knockton and Elizabeth Ellen Fleming were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Butter- market4t, and with assaulting P.C. Hardy on Monday afternoon,and Wn;h, Lauey was charged with obstructing him in the execution of his duty on the same occasion. —Hardy ,said Fleming was drunk and fighting with a woman named Daly, and he got hold of Fleming to bring her to the lock-up, when Knockton came up drunk and said he was not going to lock Fleming up and hit him twice in the face. He loosed Fleming to ~et hold of Kuockton, and Fleming got hold of him and tore his cape, and kicked him twice violently. Lacey was in their company and followed and interfered with him.— P. C. Jones corroborated.—Knockton : I should ba ashamed to give any woman the frog's march. You don't give any chance.—P.C. Jones: It would take half a dozen to take you at times.—Knockton : I was mad with drink. I did not know what I was doing.—lt ap- peared that Khockton had been convicted 42 times and discharged 11. times, and had been in jail 5 years and 3 months, and that Fleming had been convicted 30 times and discharged five. They were now each sent for two months' imprisonment with hard labour. As Knockton was being taken out of court she struck up in a loud voice a song in which occurred some references to a Warrington "bobby."—Lacey, who had been locked up at the same time as the women, was discharged.—John Win. Rutter, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge- street on Monday night, and with assaulting Robert Telford and Paulina his wife, on the same occasion. P.C. 37 said he heard screams in the street, and found the defendant drunk and that he had assaulted the Telfords. —Mr. and Mrs.Telford gave evidence. The former stated that the defendant knocked him down, and the latter that he dealt in a like manner with her on her defending him. The defendant said the former bumped against him but he denied this.—Frank Wilson corroborated.— Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, said he knew Rutter. He worked on the Ship Canal, and had hitherto borne a good character.—He was fined 53. and costs, £1 83. 6d. in all. SCITOOL CASES.—FREE Eoucivriox.—Captain Ridgway in connection with these cases asked Mr. Riley,the school attendance officer, if free education had made any differ- ence in the attendance at schools.—Mr. Riley said he did not know, but he always found that those persons who got the school fees from the Guardians were more trouble- some than anybody else.—The following persons were then dealt with for not sending their children to school : William Bottomley, fishmonger. Dial-st., 2s. 6d.; Joseph Brown, gas worker, 2s. 6d.; John Gurton, news agent, Latchford, 55.; William Quinn, labourer. School Brow, had an order made for his son to be sent to St. Anne's Industrial School; James King, baker, Angel Yard, ss. ; Frank Lee, stove maker, Guardian-st.,. 2s. 6d.; John Clare, labourer, Stamford-St. 55.; Henry Tranter, green- grocer, Enfield-st.. and William Farrington, labourer, Bewsey-road, 2s. 6d. -

WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Holmes and Councillor John Fairclough. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Catherine Benson,in Scock- ton-road, the previous night, 10s. and Costs. THURSDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton (in the chair), Major

Nicholson, and Mr. E. Gieenall. DRUNK AND BEGGING.—Thomas Hughes, drunk and begging in Church-st., the previous afternoon.—P.S. Jones proved the case. He said the man was distributing bills, and P.S. Chantler said the man had come begging to his house and insulted his wife. Some of the bills that the defendant had been distributing were handed up to the Bench, and Alderman Sutton remarked that tley were of a most objectionable character.—The defendant said a man had given him a pint of beer to distribute them. —Major Nicholson: You had no right to distribute them. They are illegal bills.—The defendant was sent to prison for 14 days' hard labour. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Warbmton, in Scot- land-road, on Wednesday night, ss. and costs. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garne.tt. (chairman) and Alder-
man Wrighi.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—EIIen Denyon, drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road, the previous afternoon, was sent to prison for 7 days. ARMY DESERTION.—George Slade, for lazing a deserter from H.M. 2nd Cheshire Regiment, stationed at Sheffield, was remanded to Strangeways jail to await an escort.. A CONVICT ON THE SPREE.—George Connolly, was charged with being drunk in Buttermarket-street, the previous night, and also that being a person under police supervision he had neglected to report himself at the police office during August and September. He was fined ss. and costs on the first charge, and on the second he was dismissed on his promising to report himself regularly in future. WOMEN'S QUARRELS.—Annie Blackburn, 53, Factory- lane, married woman, was charged with assaulting Catherine Farrington, on the 16th inst. Mr. Davies ap- peared for the complainant. The case was dismissed.— Hannah Robinson was charged with assaulting Mary Jane Dean, married woman, of Stamford-st., on Satur- day. Mr. A. Browne appeared for, Robinson, and stated thac the defendant had entered the complainant's house and got into her bedroom where she was, then threw a boot at her and cut her head severely. The place was covered with blood and the house like a slaughterhouse. She threw something at the door on going out. Evidence was called to prove the charge, and the defendant was fined ss. and costs. A FAMILY Row.—Mary Gleave, of 8, Jones's build- ings, was charged with assaulting Edward Asson, of 54. inwick-st., on the 20th inst., but dismissed. Thomas Glee ve,B, Jones's buildings, was charged with damaging a wooden dresser value 7s.the property of Hannah Asson, of 54 Winwick-se., and Hannah Asson was charged with damaging twe windows, the property of Thomas Lee. Mary Gleave and Asson were bound over in the stun of £5 and the charges of damage were dismissed. NON-MAINTENANCE.—TiIOtnaS Bate, latiourer,Old-road, Latchford, and George Dunbabbin, of Crossley-st., were charged with non-maintenance of their sons on board the Cho, and ordered to contribute is. a week each.—Thos. Lyons, fisherman, of Grimbsy. was summoned by Mr. B. Shearer, on behalf of the Guardians, for non-mainten- ance of his father, Thos. Lyons, in the Workhouse. An order for Es. per week was made. THREATENINO.—WiIIiam Matthews, ironworker, Hale- st., charged with threatening Ann Worley, his aunt, was dismissed.—John Spilsby, wiredrawer, of 38 'Leicester- st., was bound over in the sum of £5 'and mulcted in costs, 83., for threatening John Frederick Wilkinson. CRUELTY TO A Goodenough, of Fountain-St., Latchford, was charged by Inspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., with cruelty to his horse, by over- loading it, on the 16th inst. The horse, Mr. Dowty said, was in poor condition and exhausted, and the load was 3 tons 19ewt.—The Chairman said he saw from the sheet before him that the defendant was sometimes over- loaded himself.—He was fined the costs.
WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY. —Before Mr. F, H. Gossage and Mr. T. S.
DRIJNICENNESS.—For this offence a fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon Frank Stevens, no residence; Catherine Simmots, Grenfell-st. ; tJohn Starkey, Lugs-

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 26, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 26, 1891.
dale-road; ratrick DevereauN Victoria-st. ; William .Lindsey, Water-st.:; James M%hews and Richard Wil- kinson, no residence.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. TICCESDAY.—Before I.Tr. H. Gaskell and Mr. T. S. - Timmins.

MISCHLLANHOU6I—Henry Oldham, a tramp, was sen- tenced to 14 dars' hard labour for begging—For disorderly conduct Mary J. Riley, Nelson-at., who made herL2sth appearanee, was committed to gaol for 14 days.—A fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon the following for drunkenness :—Eliza Spence, Gerard-st. ; Ann Corrogan, Walmsley-st. ; Thos. Howard, Caroline-st. ; Wm. Kinsella, Elizabeth-st. ; Thos. Carr, Farrant-st. ; and Michael Varley, Bold.—Catherine Butler, Walinsley-st., was ordered to pay the costs of a summons for creating a breach of the peace. EDUCATION Acr.—Several parents were summoned for neglectinc, to send their children regularly to school, and the usual fine of ss. was iniposed iu each case. RIDING WITHOUT REINS.—Wm. Longton, Cow-lane, Ditton, pleaded guilty to this offence. ALLHGBD ASSAULT ON A WIFE.—A warrant was granted for the apprehension of Michael Windle, Locketts-row, Farnworth, on a charge of assaulting his wife. It was alleged that he had attempted to strangle her, and had stunned her by a blow on the head. THREATHNING A WATCHMAN.—Thomas Holden,of street, was charged under a warrant with using threats to Patrick Burr, watchman, of Messrs. Bolton and Son's copper works, on the 29th Juae.—The prisoner, who had absconded from the town since, was now bound over to keep the peace for three months. ASSAULTING AUNT SALLY'S' CUSTODIAN.--,Tobn ' Riley, Nelson-st., was summoned for assaulting John Horabin. On Saturday Horabin was in charge of an "Aunt Sally" stall in Pitt-st. The defendant came there drunk and took three balls without payment, and when remons- trated with, he struck Horabin on the face, knocked him down and kicked him on the mouth. The defendant was inedlOs. and costs.

Brennan returned in touch, and after 'smart passing amongst the Widnes men, the ball was carried to the visitors' goal line and a try scored by Whelan: Drum- mond, however, failed to improve upon it. The visi- tors were still getting the worst of it, and several scrim- mages took place, resulting in Widnes gaining a minor point. After splendid play had been exhibited by the Widnesians, and another minor obtained, half-time was called, the score being—Widnes 1 try 2 minors:; Dukin-, field nil. On resuming play, the game appeared a little brighter for the visitors,who eventually gained a minor: but after fine dribbling and combination play, the ball was again carriedin the visitors' quarters, and after several scrimmages had taken place, Farmer obtained a try,frorn which Barber succeeded in scoring a goal. Time was now almost up, but the ball continued near the 1 visitors' line, and a splendid try was obtained by Emery, but the attempt at goal was unsuccessful. Final Widnes, 1 goal, 2 tries, 2 minors; Dukinfield, 1 minor. The Widnes team consisted of the following :—Full-back J. Hartles ; three-quarters, D. Brennan, H. Barber, H. Peters ; hair-backs, D. Drummond, W. Mullinger ; for- wards, H. 'Farmer, G. Hewitt, J. Whelan, A. Lyons, E. Gordon, J. Hardman, J. Johnson, C. Emery, and J. 'Holmes.

RUNCORN V. ROCHDALE HORNETS. The opening match of the Runcorn season was played on Saturday, in autumnal weather, before a large crowd of spectators. Owing to the late arrival of the Hornets, it was close upon five o'clock when Faulkner started the game on behalf of Runcorn, but although a return was made, the ball was speedily back in the Rochdale half, where Evans checked an attempt to break away, and after some tine passing by Abrams and Crompton. Davies took the ball to the line,a minor point being scored. The re-start found play located in midfield ler awhile, where during a smart passage of arms, Riley bowled over Tweedale, the Hornets' full back, in grand style. At length Hirst broke away, and had almost gained the home 25 before he was brought to bay. However, Houghton relieved, and Runcorn recovered much of their lost ground. Play now, for a while, was located in the centre of the field. Whitworth also put in a good run, but being challenged, no tangible head was made. New Faulkner gave Abrams a pass, and, evading the whole of the opposing backs, the intrepid Runcornian, after crossing the line, warked his way behindthe posts, and on Crompton taking the place-kick, a fine goal was the result. Inspired by this success, the play of the homesters became more animated, Davies and Pendle- bury at this time being the most conspicuous figures on the ground. Runcorn were now well up the field, but although Tweedale faintly, returned, Houghton got up in time to make an effectual return, and now some exciting play ensued, in which Runcorn had the best of it. A moment later Abrams gave the finish to ,a fine pass from Evans, but this time Crompton's final effort did not meet with success. On re-starting, fine combination was shown by the visiting forwards, who, however, were brought up in time to prevent a dangerous development. In chase following Davies .ran splendidly, but lost the ball in a maul over the line. This was truly hard lines for the Runcern three-quarter, whn, to all appearance, fairly grounded the ball. Soon afterwards the interval was reached, when the score stood— Runcorn, 1 goal, 1 try, 2 minors; Rochdale, nil. Watson having restarted on behalf of the Hornets, play was momentarily located in the Runcorn half, where the home forwards became prominent in a passing move- ment, in which Gayter, Lea, and Williams were the actors; and by this means the play was transferred to the •visitors' 25. A cfearante, however, was speedily effected, and forthwith operations were conducted in midfield. The Hornets were now showing improved play, and the game wis much more even than before. Melladew took a free kick from a distant position in good style, bat unfortunately for the visitors the shot fell Ishort of its mark. Soon afterwards Smith kicked over the line, but, although a determined rush was made, Houghton got up in time to touch down the ball, and , possible disaster was averted. At length the Runcorn- ians pulled themselves together, but at this time open play was conSpicuous by its absence. Later on Faulkner passed to Owen Hughes, who crossed the line, amidst some excitement, but, to the surprise 'ef the crowd, the try was not allowed. Pendlebury might have taken a drop at goal, and Houghton, foolishly, allowed himself to be caught with the ball in his hands. Runcorn, how- ever, were having the best of the game, but want of tact was displayed or possibly the score might have been in- creased. The collaring all round was very smart, whilst in the packs the Hornets had somewhat the best of it, During the remaining minutes of the game the play Was mostly of a desultory character, which was diversified by a smart run by Crompton and pass to Pendlebury, who, however, was unable to break through the vigilant opposing backs. The last minute was perhaps the most exciting of the whole game, for just before the (dose Evans handed the ball to Abrams, and after Crompton had broken away, Davies received, and, racing at full speed, gained a splendidly-manceuvred try near the corner-flag. The goal-kick failed, but Runcorn had gained a well-earned victory. Final result: Runcorn, 1 , goal, 2 tries, 2 minors; Hornets, 1 minor.

yards from the line to Fair Turner, only to find the for- ward promptly pulled up before he could get thoroughly into his stride. This unselfish play was followed by Lawless being tackled with the oval in his possession, Winterbottom accounting for him. That Warrington were having the best of it must not be denied, Jolley on two occasions threatening danger. Some exchanges be- tween Barnes and Valentine eventually found Boscow beinc, called upon for the first time, and although the kick was but small it was safe, touch finding the leather a resting place at halfway. Ashton and 'Mimes were foremost in a hasty visit to the visitors' 25, and Barnes taking a pass from J. Bate forced the only minor of the match. Immediately after the drop out, J. Bate tricked Bumby well, but Murray was safe, and cleared his lines and Barnes in trying to force an open- ing found an obstacle in Marsh. Swinton now had a turn, Sharpies, Walker, and Hotchkiss all being prominent on their side assuming the agres- tive. A rush took the oval under the post, where scrimmages rendered • the game monotonous. A tackle by Barnes of Marsh gave relief, and Fair Turner and Bandies in turn taking up the movement Warrington again attacked. Near the call of half time Valentine was afforded a chance. but Evans judging his man grandly , pulled him up, and when the interval arrived the homes- ters had scored i minor to nil. _ _ _

On resuming, as in the first portion, exchat3ge kicks to the number of six marked the opening items.. The first to show up was Jolley, who cleared Walker from his path, but some slight infringement spoiled his progress. Smart dribbling by Holmes, Dimohue. Fair Turner, and Jolley was taken up by Lawless, but the tackling, which had not been of a gentle descriistion on both sides, ac- counted for his being speedily pulled up. A wild pass by Berry was taken advantage of by Hall, who got the oval away to Boscow, the latter being safe as ever. Still playing pluckily, the visitors gained a 'footing well in home quarters, Rsthwell and Hallam being prominent on two occasions. Marsh was too well cared for to become dangerous, and the ball only travelled from touch to touch. From a long throw out Randles had possession, and another unique spell of passing ruled the game at half way, a rare round of applause greeting the last performers. Swinton had the better of a pack opposite the grand stand, and a few short exchanges found Winterbottom making tracks for the line. Evans tackled well, and from this point, Swinton had shot their bolt. True, Valentine made a grand run along the popular side, but Boscow had alway the measure of him. On the other hand,Marsh was decidedly at fault,and J. Bate dribblinc, a trifle too hard found Murray trying ineffectively to round Evans. The home forwards headed by their skipper, forced the play, and after Murray hactsaved his lines more than once, a kick to Valentine saw the "mere sprinter "-mulling the ball, with the result that from the pack which followed J. r. Bate was a trifle too clever for Brockbank, and wriggling through gained an unmistak- able try. Cheers and waving of hats and other sundries greeted the homesters' success, and these were renewed when Barnes placed the goal. Only a few minutes were now required to brinc, the game to a close, but during that time Evans obliged with a strong run. Marsh was slightly hurt near the call of time, but when the whistle sounded "No side" Warrington had won a hard fought game by a goal and a minor to nil. Teams :—Warrington : Boscow, back ; Lawless, T. Barnes, and J. W. Evans, three-quarter backs ; James Bate and John Bate, half back; Ashton, Fair Tuiner, Randles, Berry, E. Dillonl Nevins, Jolley, Holmes, and Donohue, forwards. Swinton ;Murray, back; Valentine, Marsh, and Winterbottom, three-quarter backs ; Bumby and Brockbank, half backs; N. Hotchkiss, Hall, Hallam Evans, G. S'narples, A. Sharpies, Rothwell, Evans, and J. Hotchkiss, forwards.

div.p: RUNCORN pErrY SESSIONS,

MownAy.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. Charles Reynolds. BRIIIMENNESS.—Wm. Sutton, for being drunk at Frodsham Bridge was fined ss. and costs; and for a like offence at Weston, John Wilding was fined ss. and costs. A PALTRY SQUABBLE.—Mary Ellison' of Bentinck-st., was summoned for assaulting Mary Ann Bartlett, of TreEtham-street.—Mr. Burton appeared for the com- plainant and Mr. Humphreys for the defendant. It appeared that the entry from the complainant' S house ran past the defendant's house, and on Saturday the 12th inst., a pool of water settled there through the defendant swilling her flags. Complainant brought a riddle and some ashes to the place, intending to riddle the ashes there, but the defendant threw a bucket of water upon them,wettinci Mrs. Bartlett's feet and clothes. Several witnesses corroborated this allegation. The de- fence was a direct denial of the charge. The defendant's daughter said the water was thrown to lay the dust caused by the riddling. The dust caused them to have to clean again the lobby and stairs.—Other witnesses having been heard, Mr. Brundrit said it was a pity so much time should have been spent over such a paltry case. A fine of is., and costs 14s. was imposed. STRRET OBSTRUCTION.—WiIIiam Bailey, a Ship Canal labourer, was charged with obstructing the footpath in Church-st., on Saturday afternoon, and waslined 23.63. and costs, or 7 days. Tram OF A JACRET.—Thorn as Uichrrds, young man, a stranger, was charged with haying, on the 113th Sept., stolen a jacket, value 203., from the shop door of Messrs. Robertson and Son, clothiers, Bridge-st.—Fred. Kersley, the assistant, deposed to the. jacket being missing.—P.S. Gosling said he saw the prisoner in Mr. Craddock's pawnshop, with the jacket in his possession. In answer to his •questions the prisoner said he had bought the jacket on the previous day, at Manchester, .and paid 355. for it. Afterwards, when charged at the Police Station, the prisoner said he had purchased the jacket from a navvy.—The prisoner was remanded fora week in order that inquiries might be made as to his antecedents.

A GUILTY Boy.—John Thompson, a boy, pleaded guilty to havina,on Saturday evening,stolen from a stall on the market a tobacco pipe worth 6d., the property of John Owen. He was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod-at the hands of a P.C.

A VIOLENT TRAMP.—John Lynch,a tramp,was charged with begging and also assaulting P.C. Hughes, on Satur- day afternoon. Hughes was on duty in plain clothes, when the prisoner came and asked him for alms. He told him he was a police constable and then took him into custody. On the way to the police station the prisoner kicked him on the legs and otherwise assaulted him.— For begging the prisoner was sentenced to 7 days' hard labour and for the assault to 14 days' hard labour.

div.p: RUGBY.

WARRINGTON RANGERS V. RUNCORN RECREATION ( A TEAMS) .—This match was played at Warrington on Saturday afternoon, and the final result was—Rangers, 2 tries (Deakin and Heft) ; Recreation, 1 try. WARRINGTON STAR V. RUNCORN HORNETS.—These promising teams played on Saturday afternoon, at Warrington. Floyd and Barratt scored. Final result: —Warrington, 1 goal 1 try 2 minors ; Runcorn 1 minor. WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH V. RUNCORN TRUE BLVES.—A grand game between these clubs on Saturday resulted in a draw, the tries being scored by Threadgold and Mason. Morgan, J. Warburton, and Cliff played well for Parish Church, and Threadgold and several forwards for Runcorn. Final result :—True Blues, 1 try; Parish Church, 1 try. PROUST:IAM 17. WARRINGTON 2ND.—This match was played at Warrington on Saturday. The Frodsham team were minus Goodall and Clough. At the start the game was fairly even, but Frodsham soon began to show up, and T. Darlington gained a well-earned try. The same player took the place kick, but failed. Play then con- tinued even up to half time. In the second 'half, Frodsham had much the best of the play, mid T. Brown scored an unimproved try. About two minutes from , time the home centre dropped a goal, thus eoualizing the , score, which was—Frodsharn two tries to Warrington 2nd one goal (dropped). Parker, Peacock, Brown, and Darlington played a good game for the visitors. 1 WARRINGTON" A" v. SWINTON " A."—At Swinton, on Saturday. Warrington kicked off, and a bad pass was fully utilized by the Swinton forwards, and away went the game into Warrington territory, but relief came when Lawless and Molyneaux came gallantly through. This effort was followed by Buckley getting finely away and throwing to Thornley, whose pass was missed, and the homesters raced to the centre line. After some sterling work, in which Rowlands, Teare, and Knowles were noticeable, Antrobus got away and threw to Heesom, who handed to Potts, the latter being tackled in close proximity to the line. Potts directly after was again prominent, and, following a lot of exciting play, Harris ran capitally to midfield. The game was now fast and exciting, and Sampson, who throughout played grandly, evoked cheers by twice clearing his lines. A series of passes by the visitors' backs harassed the home defence, but Swinton retaliating, Wilson looked like scoring, Sampson effecting a good tackle. The attackers were in turn defenders, as Lawless dashed away with the leather, and a vigorous onslaught by the Warrington team ended in Knowles rushing over. The kicking abilities of the respective backs were again ex- hibited, and Lawless running finely started a lot of pass-. ing among the Warrington forwards near the goal line. A fine chance was, however, missed, and Swinton, by the aid of Marsden and Green, effected a good relief. Some splendid kicking by Sampson ensued, and Barns by a run and kick forcing his opponents back. This being supplemented by some strong forward play by Thornley, Bailey, Warburton, and Molyneaux, found the combat in close proximity to the home goal. A kick by Daniels travelled over the line, but Rothwell riskily punted out, and Sampson seiting the leather al- most secured a try by a grand bit of work. A pass by Knowles to Heesom enabled the centre to make a beauti- ful dodgy run, clean through his opponents, and he ex- perienced hard lines in not scoring. Marsden and Green were the means of getting the ball out Of danger, and Wilson immediately after got right away, only to see Barnes come across and effect a fine tackle. Swinton continued to press their attentions on the •goal, but ul- timately some capital passing between Antrobus, Hee- som, and Potts, enabled the latter to gain a try, which was disallooked, and half-time arrived, with Warrington one try to nil. After the usual interval, Swinton re- sumed, and a run and pass by Lawless put his antagon- ists on the defensive. Barnes then came through with the ball at his toes, only to see Rothwell clear. Buckley, and Knowles by combined dribble frustrated their op- ponents, and Lawless dashed away to the quarter-flag. Daniels then had a chance, which he utilised by dribbl- ing splendidly over,and Heesom kicked a goal. The game tamed down considerably after this, and Swinton were quickly forced back with a dashing run by Buckley. A series of tall kicks between the rival backs was wit- nessed, and Warburton, Molyneaux, Teare, and Bailey rushed to the line. The home team were having all the worst of the fray, and although Hotchkiss temporarily relieved, Antrobus soon had the ball bobbing near the line. A very fine piece of play by Harris and Wilson sent the leather right to the Warrington line. The stay was but temporary, as Warburton, Bailey, Buckley, and Rowlands dashed away to midfield, and a long kick by Potts went into touch in the Swinton half. A nice spell of passing between Teare, Thornley, and Knowles was succeeded by a grand rush of the whole of the Warring- ton forwards, and Daniels, picking up smartly, dropped a grand goal. Restarting, the game proceeded in an uninteresting fashion, but eventually Harris got clean away, only to be floored by Sampson. Lawless was hurt at this stage, and had to retire, and a long- drop at goal ny Wilson notched a minor. Nothing further was scored, and Warrington retired winners by 2-1-0 to 0-0-1.

div.head: WARRINGTON V. STOCKPORT.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. STOCKPORT.

• These teams met at Stockport on Monday afternoon in miaerable weather. There would be fully 5,000 present, when the homestera, who' had the assistance of Donald Jowett, Wharton, and Saville, all of Heekmondwlke, kicked off. Saville's kick was responded to by James Bate, and Evans having the reply charge, the Stock port men were at the Warrington end when the first scrimmage was formed. Thornley headed the visitors in a speedy excursion to the Cheshire end, and ex- changes between Saville and Boscow ended with advan- tage to the homester. A spell of uninteresting give-and- take play Was followed by a grand movement on the part of the Warrington half backs, James Bate running and passing finely to Barnes, who slipped when a grand chance of scoring was presented him. Dain, who had apparently a roving commission, eased the pressure,' but again J. Bate became prominent with a fine kick. Ashton, Turner, and Berry bore ridown on the ho'me goal, and Murray being hotly pressed, his kick was but a . faint response to one by ,Evans. The game was now being contested under the most unpleas- ant conditions, rain falling in torrents, the .large crowd presenting a sorry spectacle. Despite this , drawback,the play was watched with interest; and the ' home enthusiasts cheering a fine forward display headed by Donald Jowett, went almost frantic when Saville all but landed a goal from a penalty kick. Barnes ran the oval out, and aided by the fine play of Evans and Ash- ton, Warrington again attacked. Another capital dis- play by the two Bates was frustrated by Saville intercept- ing a pass intended for Barnes, and Stockport again breathed more freely. J. T. Bate showed up prominently in a dribble through the opposing, backs, but Randles overran the oval, and Lawless eventually put in a fine run in response to a tall kick by Fleet. Ashton got clear from a line-out, but was grassed before he travelled far. J. Bate next got over, but the phint was disallowed, but fortune favoured an effort by Fair Turner a few moments later, for securing from a line-out he was soon in his stride, and running strongly he defied the efforts of Murray to check him, finally scoring in a favour- able position,. .Barnes failing to augment. Follow- ing the restart, J. Bate forced a minor, whilst Boscow accounted for a second. J. Bate again out- witted the Stockport men with his smart play, and an- other long run along touch and pass to Lawless saw Murray tackling the latter firmly. A third minor fell to Warrington's credit, this being the outcome of smart forward play on the part of Daniels, Donohue, and Turner. Near the call of half-time the visitors made a bold bid for a major point, the final issue, and the score read at the interval—Warrington, .0-1-2 ; Stockport, nil. The play during the second half was marred by the incessant rain, the players being scarcely able to obtain a firm footing. Stockport had a shade the best of the first twenty minutes, but the defence was good and a minor was the Cheshire men's only reward. Near the close the visitors showed superior stamina, and the last quarter was confined to the home quarters. James Bate had a grand try disallowed, a decision that did not meet with the approval of an impartial crowd. Two more minors fell to the credit of Warrington, and the game ended as follows :—Warrington 0-1-5, Stockport 0 -0-1. , WARRINGTON V. SWINTON.

Fresh from their victories over the Isle of Man and St. Helens Recreation teams, tike Warrington and Swinton clubs brought the first of their annual engagements to an issue on Saturday afternoon at Wilderspool. The great interest taken in the match, not only by the res- pective partizans of both clubs, but by a wide area, naturally accounted for the large attendance, which must have been considerably over 6,000 when the game was started. Previous matches—four in all—had resul- ted in each club winning on their own heath, but War- rington claimed the credit of having inflicted the heavi- est defeat.

The teams were similar to those which had performed so successfully the week before, and an unexpected punctual start having been made, the excitement was at its highest in a very short time. Nevins set the oval in motion, and some neat exchanges taking place between Valentine and Evans, neither side claimed any advan- tage at the. close of the operations. Aft% some manceuvring by both sets-of forwards, the twolßates, Barnes, and Evans got the oval woiking amongst them, but the Swinton defence was grand, and Brockbank in an ace had the oval out of danger". Randles soon re- gained the lost ground, and Ashton tackling well, the visitors had a shade the worst of the argument. The home forwards were playing a wonderful game for a team which many thought, was out of condition and to show that this . was an illusion, they pushed their opponents with ,ease. After an exciting incident, Valentine, Rothwrell, and Marsh got well away to the quarter flag. Nevins staving off the attempt to clear with an accurate save, and another spell of passing by the home backs saw Lawless trying a shot at goal. The faint effort was promptly met, and Murray, assisted by Bumby, Hallam, and Hall, for the first time gained a , footing inside the home quarters. A smart run by Evans was applauded, but the cheers were deafening a moment later when he snapped up a pass intended by Marsh for Valentine, and handed over the charge when but five

div.head: TRAGIC DEATH OF A BOY.
div.p: TRAGIC DEATH OF A BOY.

The coroner for East Surrey on Wednesday received information of the death of Otta Post, 16, ship's boy of the barque Dazic, lying in dock at Rotherhithe. On Tuesday afternoon the master, named Branroff. was standing upon one of the beams doing some repairs, when the deceased shouted to him, "You look like God in heaven stuck up there." Branroff, it is alleged. threw a chisel at the lad, striking him in the thigh. Post died 20 minutes aftetwards. Branroff is in custody.

div.head: MURDER BY BOYS.
div.p: MURDER BY BOYS.

The inquest on the body of David Dawson Eccles, the boy who was drowned in the cellar of an unfinished building in Victoria-st., in Liverpool, was resumed on Wednesday. It will be remembered that two boys named Samuel Crawford and Robert Sheernan confessed that they had induced deceased to strip for bathing, and had drowned him in order that they might steal his clothes. A verdict of "Wilful murder" was returned against the two boys, who were committed for trial on the coroner's warrant.

div.head: MINING DISASTER IN BELGIUM.
div.p: MINING DISASTER IN BELGIUM.
LOSS OF 27 LIVES.

A terrible colliery accident is announced from Forchies, in the province of Hainault, where a formidable explo- sion of fire damp occurred at three o'clock on Saturday afternoon at the Monceau Fontaine Mine. Twenty-seven men, who were at work at the time on a landing at a depth of about 350 yards, were all killed in the catas- trophe which is attributed to atmospheric depression, as the pieties always been held to be one of the safest in the country. The explosion was preceded by a prolonged subterranean rumbling, which caused consternation in the whole locality, and the fearful report caused by the explosion brought all the inhabitants in a few moments to the mouth of the pit. Rescue parties were at once or- ganized, and miners off duty volunteered to go down in search of their comrades. It was not long before news reached the pit's mouth that the effects of the explosion had been very deadly, and soon after the bodies of the victims began to be brought to the surface. The greater number of the twenty-seven men who perished were married, and there were most distressing scenes at the head of the shaft, as the wives identified the bodies-of their dead husbands. By half-past ten all the corpses and several injured miners-had been brought up. The colliery where the disaster occurred comprises five pits, in which 2,700 men are employed.

Sydney Old, late secretary of the Wallsend Pontoon and Dry Docks Company, Limited, who absconded in June last, has been arrested in New York on a charge of em- bezzling £5,000. Two negro "land boomers" have been killed near Langston, Oklahoma. A woman who passed over the boundary line before the prearranged time shot at one of the deputy marshals who had called her back, and he in return shot her in the leg, incapacitating her from join- ing in the rush.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
A.TALETICS.
MISCELLANEOITS.

Mr. J. B. Radcliffe, a well-known Newcastle journalist, has accomplished a very remarkable all-round feat. Be had matched himself for various bets to row a quarter of a mile, swim the same distance, run 440 yards, ride a bicycle over the same course,‘Laftd ride a horse a quarter of a mile, all within the space of fifteen minutes. Mr,. Ratcliffe easily accomplished the five tasks in the allotted time, with 2 mins. 12 secs. to spare. Mr. Radcliffe's general proficiency in athletics was well known amongst his many friends, while, in addition to being a good sculler and swimmer, he is also a very capable golfer.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Salford came a " cropper" on Saturday, and there seemed to be a peculiar fitness in St. Helens being the cause of their fall. Sudlow was last season the "Saints" crack three-quarter, but now every Saturday leaves the smoke and" chemic " loehind fora few, hours' enjoyment with the "Reds," and the Saints" don't like it much. Hosker having returned to Blackley, the " Reds " wanted another half-back, and the hospitality of the Salfordians is now so famous at St. Helens that the fact,that France, who played for the St. ,Helens Recreation a week ago and was,solected for last Satur- day, was discovered partnering Walsh at New Barnes will not create much wonder.

Pilkington, the St. Helens Reci:eation captain and half back, has, through .an injury to his ribs, had to be a looker-on at the last two Saturday's matches. He will take his place in the team at Millom next week, and the " mainspring " restored, the club are hoping to score a long list of uninterrupted victories.

Not the least interesting feature in connection with the meeting of the Lancashire County F.C. last week was the announcement made by Mr. Hornby that last season's champion fifteen would be. presented by medals. This recognition is well deserved ,and it 'xVoulir have been a pity to have let the occasion 'go by without making it.

Perhaps, with two exceptions, the seven League battles of Saturday came out as anticipated. The exceptions were the matches at Bolton and Preston. Sunderland would not have astonished anybody had they won at Pike's-lane, and the success of the North End against the Villa would have been accepted as a verification of form. As it happened, however, both the Wanderers and the " Villans " were in fine fettle, and still pose as the only unbeaten members of the League. The Birmingham team are an easy first on the goal average, their colours having only been twice lowered, whilst they -have totted up eleven points.

The Notts club had over 1,000 members the day they played at Preston, and since then they have issued 500 more member's tickets. Notts Forest says they have over 1,300 members, too. And;yet trade is bad in Nott- ingham!

Rugby players must not forget that scoring under the new system comes into force at once, as does the altera- tion in the rules as regards dead ball. Players will there- fore will do well to make themselves thoroughly acquainted with the same. Under the new code, a try counts 2 points ;.a, penalty goal, 3 points; a dropped goal or goal kicked from a rolling ball, 4 points ; a goal kicked from a try, 5 points.

The Warrington team will mot often have to fight a tougher battle than they did on Saturday .with Swinton. The play of Saturday, as , did the matches of last year, showed that the two combinations are as nearly equal as possible, though it is only fair to say that the home team had on the whole rather the better of the play, just as they had of the score. It is quite clear from the form displayed by Warrington on Saturday and on Monday against Stockport that they are in something like in yin- cible form<this season. If they can manage to play with some degree of regularity their full team, it is quite within the range of probability that they may go through the season unbeaten.

div.head: BOWLS.
div.p: BOWLS.

• .BOWLING MAIN AT CROFT.—On Saturday the mem- bers of the byirling, club held at the Shepherds' Inn, Lowton, journeyed to the Horseshoe Inn, Croft, and played a main of bowls. THE NORTHEAST MANCHESTER VACANCY.'

Tuesday night's "Gazette "announces that Sir tames Fergusson was on Tuesday in the presence of the Right Hon. Henry Matthews, M.P., one of her Majesty's prin- cipal secretaries of State, sworn Postmaster-General. The Liberals of North-East Manchester, have deter- mined on opposing the Postmaster-General. On Tues- day evening, a meeting of the Council of the North-East Manchester Liberal Association was held, Mr. Alderman Holland (Liberal candidate for North Salford), president of the association,in the chair. Three-fourths of the 200 members who comprise the Council were present. On the motion of Mr. County Alderman Forrest, seconded by Mr. Alderman George Evans, it was unanimously de- cided to invite Mr. C. P. Scott, editor of the "Manches- ter Guardian," to contest the division. Mr. Scott, who was present, accepted the invitation, and delivered an address. The proceedings were marked with greaten- thusiasm, and the work of the contest will be com- menced at once.

Mr. Scott, who is now fairly in the field as the Liberal candidate, contested the division against Sir James Fergusson in 1886,and he then reduced the sitting mem- ber's majority of 1,448 in 1885 to 327. Since then he has been active in the prosecution of sanitary reform in the division, which comprises the unhealthy district of Ancoats and has gained a popularity which will make him a Arong candidate. The Conservatives say that their organisation is in excellent order,and it is probable that in this respect they have an advantage over their opponents. Sir James Fergusson will address his first meeting on Monday. The nominations will probably take place on the 3rd October, and the polling on the 9th of October.

Sir James Fergusson will not, accordipg to present arrangements, begin his campaign in North-east Man- chester before Monday, but his opponent kMr. C. P. Scott) held his first meeting on Thursday night in Isling- ton New Hall, and was cordially received.

div.head: MR. JOHN 31ORLEY AT CAMBRIDGE.
div.p: MR. JOHN 31ORLEY AT CAMBRIDGE.
Mr. John Morley addressed a crowded meeting in the

)Cambridge Guildhall, on Monday night, as president of 'the Cambridge and County Liberal Club. He said that at the approaching general election there would be no party or banner of Dissentient Liberalism, but the fight would be a straight one between Liberals and Tories. The Conservatives would base their appeal on foreign policy, constructive statesmanship, and pacification of Ireland. He proceeded to examine and dispute their claim under each of these heads. The whole cost and risk of our persistent and indefinite occupation of Egypt should be recognised. The English Local Government Bill was a mere skeleton' and the Free Education Bill 'had not done more than touch the fringe of the question, which could not be settled without effective popular re- presentative control of the schools. The Irish Land Pur- chase Act was a monument rather of destructive than of constructive statesmanship, and the extreme safeguards and restrictions of all kinds predicted to accompany the Irish Local Government Bill next session would still further prolong and embitter Irish controversies in Par- liament. Although differing from the majority in the recent Trades Union Congress on the eight hours ques- tion he hailed the discussions of that Congress with hope and satisfaction, having every confidence in the sound- ness of the ultimate judgment of working-men in seek- ing to improve their own welfare. Criticising the recent speech of Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, at Trowbridge, he ridiculed that speaker's hard-mouth Toryism, and ad- vocated village con ncils,in which the rural classes should have the management of their own charities, manage- ment of allotments under the Act, powers over public buildings and common land, as well as powers for com- pulsory acquisition of land for public objects. But in order to clear the way for social reforms, the Liberal, party must first fulfil their Home Rule pledges.

div.head: COAL MINES REGULATION ACT.
div.p: COAL MINES REGULATION ACT.

Two cases under the Coal Mines Regulation Act were heard before Messrs. W. L. M'Clure and R. A. Gladstone, at Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday. • In the first case, Ralph Lyon, a stoker at Prescot Colliery, belonging to the Wigan and Whiston Coal Company, was summoned for failing to keep certain appliances and machinery in..good order.—Mr. J. 0. Swift (St. Helen's) Pirdsecuted, hind stated that defendant was in charge of three boilers, in cpnnection with which there was a super-heater or another boiler into whiclfthe exhaust steam from the other boilers was passed. It was absolntely necessary that this machinery should be kept in proper order, but on Monday, the 31st August, whilst ' some men were ,descending the pit-shaft the end ,of one of the cylinders was blown out. This caused the winder to practically lose control over his winding; the engine suddenly stopped, and some injury was done to the machinery. The men irrthe shaft received a considerable shock, and were naturally terrified. It,was afterwards ascertained that the defendant had illegally placed a plug in the overflow pipe from the boilers, and his explanation was that he had forgotten to remove it.—William Gerrard, , manager, said he spoke to the defendant after the occurrence, and he was told that the water had got 'rather low, and defendant put in the plug; intending to remove it when sufficient water had been got it.—John Haslam, the engine Ni-inder, stated that he was lowering eight men down the shaft in ,one cage and the other cage was ascending with other eight men._ 16 being in the , shaft together, when the engine suddenly stopped. It caused the cages to give a sudden "chuck," and witness had no proper control over the engines until the damage ' had been temporarily 'repaired.— Defendant said he had been cursed several times about water running from the overflow pipe, and he put in the plug, intending to remove it afterwards.—The bench considered the offence a serious one, but took a very lenient 'view, and imposed a fine of £1 and costs.—Two colliers, named John Hughes and Frank Halford, also employed at Prescot Colliery, were charged with ascending the pit shaft con- trary to instructions and orders.—Mr. Swift stated that colliers were not allowed to asend the mine contrary to instructions during the periods for winding coal.—Mr. Wilson, of Wigan, who defended, elicited frotn the wit- nesses that the defendants had complained about the condition of their working • place on the previous day. They had complained that it was unsafe, but the colliery officials stated that examinations proved the place to be perfectly safe.—Mr. Wilson submitted that the offence was of a trivial character, and the bench imposed a nominal fine of 2s. 6d. and costs upon each defendant.

THE FINANCES OF THE UNION.

The Clerk submitted the estimates for the corning half year. In doing so he said the estimate of Unicn receipts and expenditure for the second or winter half of the finan- cial year 1891-2 is based on the usual calculations, duo regard being also paid to prevailing conditions. Abnor- mal sickness and a high death rate have been attended by increase of outlay under the heads of in-maintenance and out-relief. The cost of lunatics 'at asylums was fixed at a higherrate per week than in the last year. Additions and structural alteration of workhouse buildings were needed. Exceptional changes made in the official staff had caused exceptional expense; a small addition had also been made to the salaries account. After providing for these and for ordinary Union disbursements the com- mon charges, distributed over the 16 parishes in propor- tion to their rateable, were fixed at £5,064 averaging a fraction over 4d in the £. The estimated expenditure under the head of common charges for the present or summer half year was £5,877, or a fraction also over 4d. in the £. In response to the demands by County Councils a sum of £4.537 would have been paid, within the year, to Lancashire and Cheshire. Whatever room there might yet be for the exercise of economy by Lancashire, the townships of the Union within it fared better than do those within Cheshire. Grappenhall and Th,elwall were jointly rated (parochially) at £12,002 the County charges being £343 for the year. Cuerdley and Penketh, equally adjacent, and jointly rated (parochially) at £12,866, Day the county £216. If they took Poulton and Win wick. jointly rated (parochially) at tbe much higher sum of £17,207 they found their total payment to the County be £283 or £65 less than by Grappenhall and Thelwail for the same period. Their calls upon parishes in 1889- 90 were £18,217 (a less sum than for the previous year) and in 1890-1 £15,804. me call for the expiring hale year was £8,22r. That now advised was £7,506, or £15,727 for the year. In the three preceding years the Union rateable value stood at £319.699, £328,633 and £329,052. The present total was £336,464. div.head: SELECTED READINGS.
div.p: SELECTED READINGS.

ANDBEW CARNEGIE. —David Brooks was manager of a PiAtsburg railroad office,when a boy named Andrew Carnagie was a messenger in it at a salary of three dollars a week. The boy had just arrived with his father and mother from Scotland, the land of his birth. That was a very little More than 36 years.ago, yet to-day he is the famous millionaire ironmonger of Pittsburg. Andrew Carnegie has said —" I owe my rise in life to a game of checkers." I will explain to you what that remark means. The elder Carnegie was a moulder in a pottery. Like .many Sotchmen, be was exceedingly fond of play- ing checkers. In Pittsburg at that time was a well known ale house, in one room of which those who loved to play checkers were wont to assemble. Among them were Carnegie and Brooks, and in this way the two men became acquainted. Carnegie's eon also came there at times with his father, and, he too, tested David Brooks' powers at draughts. One day the elder Carnegie re- marked that he did not know what to do with his son. "Send him down to my office, and I will make a messenger boy of him," said. Mr. Brooks. The next day he began his new' employment. The lad was intelligent and industrious. Manager Brooks had an old telegraph instrument fitted up in his office, and when the mestenger boys were not engaged he showed them on this how to tick out the Morse alphabet. With this instruction young Carnegie soon became a skilful operator. Thomas A. Scott was at that time Superintendent of the rermsylvania Railroad in Pittsburg. He had a telegraph instrument rigged up in his office and wanted some one to manipulate the key. Manager Brooks recommended young Carnegie, and be was employed. He showed such iptitude in managing the movement of trains 14 telegraph that be was transferred to the superintendent's office in Altoona. There he continued to attract the attention of Thomas A. Scott, and was rapidly pushed along. was given opportunities to engage in some coal and oil speculations that were successful, and after- ward made money from the first sleeping cars that
were built.

-- THZ EMPEROR NICHOLAS AND THE ENGLISH COURT.—Nicholas quitted London on the. 9th of gune, 1844, after producing a very good impression on the ladies and gentlemen of the Court by his magnificent presents of jewels to the former, and, as regarded the latter, by the gift of a very valuable cup,' to be annually run for at Ascot, which he had visited twice during his brief stay. Whether he produced an equally good impression on the mass of the English people is a very doubt- ful matter. It was said at the time that he was hissed on one occasion when driving out with the 'Queen, and it was probable that such was the fact. Be was disliked as a despot; his conduct towards 'Poland was viewed with detestation; and that he had designs on India was suspected and believed :by many. But his reception at the English Court was sufficiently warm to create a feeling of irrita- tion on the part of the French, who inferred—not altogether without reason that some secret arrangement had been made to the prejudice of their interests. It was feared for a time that this sentiment would have the effect of setting aside a visit to England which had been contemplated by 'Louis Philippe since the visit of the Queen and Prince Albert to that Monarch iii the previous year. Alluding to the fear that this compliment Knight not be paid, in consequence of what had happened with the Emperor, Her Majesty, in writing to King Leopold, says:—" I hope that you will persuade the King (Louis Philippe) to come all the same in September. Our motives and politics are not to be exclusive, but to be on good terms with all—and why should we not? We make no secret of it." The King, of Saxony left England on the 19th of June, and the Court now returned to its usual and somewhat quiet routine. —The Life and Times of Queen Victoria. BEN Joiesow's TRAINING.—Of all the playwrights who were his contemporaries, Ben Jonson was the only born Londoner. If we except the brief episode of his soldiering in the Low Countries, he had hardly quitted the purlieus of the Tower and Westminster. His time as a boy passed between severe studies at school and perambulations in the City streets. Though the country at that period neighboured so closely on the capital that an active lad might escape into the fields between school hours, yet the dominant influences of Jonson's growing years were far from rural. Town-bred and bred to scholarship, he underwent influences very different from those which shaped the mind of Shakespeare in his home at Stratford. We ought not to insist too crudely on this con- trast. Temperament must in all cases be reckoned snore powerful than education, and it may be remembered that Keats was a cockney. Yet no one will contend the brilliant parallel drawn by Swinburne between Bartholomew Fair and the Merry Wives of Windsor, the purely farcical masterpieces of the town-bred schoolboy and the country lad, is overstrained. Jonson, exploring the classics with Camden for his guide, in the hey- day of the English Renaissance, formed an idea of art different from that of his great comrade, who learned small Latin and less Greek under the ferule of some village Holofernes. Hours of leisure passed among the wherries of the Thames developed sensibilities and powers of observation in Jonson alien to those which expanded in the soul of Shakespeare upon the banks of Avon, or in the glades of Charlecote.—English Worthies, by J. A. Symonds. THERE is something queer in the fact that a man does not like to go out of his way. You ask a man how far it is to Greenville; and he tells you ten miles, you can drive that distance and not get particularly tired. But if he tells you that it is four miles, but the river is up and you will have to fo two miles out of your way, making eight miles an all, you will think it the longest eight miles you ever rode in your life. When you get within two miles of Greenville you will say that if you had not had to have gone out of your way you would be • there now, and that the light is not conducive to one's patience, I as not fond of denouncing my fellow-sinners, but gambling . . . stirs my disgust even more than my pity. The sight of the dull faces ,bending round the gaming-tables, the raking tip of the money, and the flinging of the coins towards the winners by the hard-faced croupiers; the hateful, hideous women staring at the board like stupid mono-maniacs—all this seems to me the most abject presentation of mortals grasping after something called a good that can be seen on the face of this little earth. Burglary is heroic com- pared with it.—George Eliot. No cowardice is so great as that found in want of truth. Belief in the rightness of a cause, in the value of a high moral, standard, in the supreme righteousness overruling man, self-respect and moral dignity—all go by the board when we con- descend to a lie either spoken or acted, either by suggestion of the false or suppression of the truth. Whatever it may be that we are called on to testify or acknowledge we should stand to openly and without wincing. SELF-POSSESSION is an important element of a successful manner—" Be self-possessed; that is the only art of life," ,says lotephistopheles to Faust—and shyness or self-consciousness is, more than anything-else, detrimental to ease of manner. This, commonest of defects, which may be largely increased or eounteracted by early influences and training, is however in many cases constitutional and unconquerable. THERE is as much merit in catering to the humorous side of our nature as to the sober and sedate. Men and women were made to laugh and indulge in pleasantries just as much as to fast and pray. Because a face is uncommonly long instead of wide, it does not follow that its possessor is a first-class saint. We would as soon trust a coun- tenance got up on the broad as the long gauge. CLAUDE LORRAINE, the great landscape painter, was originally apprenticed to a pastry cook. When he first went to Rome he was so destitute of resources that he was glad to act as cook and colour- grinder to the painter Tassi, and he thus secured the means of pursuing the art in which he after- wards attained so rare an eminence. IT is injurious to be in a hurry, and delay is often equally so; he is wise who does everything In proper time. Tardiness and precipitation are extremes equally to be avoided. - LET US pit plenty of life into our existence, plenty of work into our life, plenty of heart into our work, and plenty of warmth into our heart.-- -BPurgeon.

RUNCORN CHAPELS.

Sir,—l should like. to point out that your conies- pondent of last week is mistaken in stating that Bethesda Chapel is the oldest in Runcorn. St. John's is the oldest. It was built in 184 ; Brunswick, now used as a Sunday School, comes next, built in 1827, then St. Luke's built in 1839, and then liethesda, built in 1835.—Yours faith- J.S.
'Runcorn, 23rd September.
PRAYER FOR FAIR WEATHER.

Sir,—At the time of, and commenting upon the bac- carat case, one of your correspondents made some gratui- tous and not over pertinent remarks concerning the, as he hinted, inefficacy of the church's prayer for "Albert Edward Prince of Wales." Last Sunday but one the church offered prayer for fair weather. A week of most glorious weather followed. If your correspondent is logical and just he will perhaps kindly note this. Of course Ido not concur in the way in which your correspondent regards prayer, which he evidently values in proportion to its answer, but it struck me that the above fact might suit his reasoning. The church duly made her thanksgiving last Sunday, a course which I trust your correspondent will approve. /a Mark Twain, I would remind your correspondent that he forgot to say if the Prinro'a conduct and charac- ter might not have been worse had no prayers ever been offered in his hohalf.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, H. T. W. Stockton Eeath, 14th Sep., 1891.

div.head: LICENSING AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: LICENSING AT WARRINGTON.
"To be forewarned is to be forearmed."

Sir,-1 am told that when the Licensing Committee of magistrates retired on Tuesday, to consider the question of granting another out-door license they wfshed to ex- press, through the Mayor, their: intention next year to re-arrange the various licenses by establishing new ones in Battersby-lane and Bewsey-road, and closing others in Buttermarket-st. lam a local optionist, and if the in- habitants of these districts require such places by all means let them have them; but as I believe the vast majority of the people hare no wish to increase " the overgrown power of the liquor interest," let them in the coming Municipal and Parliamentary elections show by their votes that they are determined that an irrespon- sible body like the Warrington magistrates shall no longer injure the moral and physical welfare of the people ; but advance with the times and carry out in a proper spirit a reduction of the pest houses planted in our midst.
A RADICAL J.P.
THE TEACHINGS OF THEOSOPHY.

Sir,—Having read your article in last week's issue on Theosophy, I shall feel obliged if you will permit me to state that its teachings are based on natural and not on super-natural phenomena,and it is by these that it ought to be judged. We cannot afford to abandon the truth wheresoever we find it, because others who believe the game truth add thereto a belief in phenomena which we do not credit. Tne question is—Are the teachings of Theosophy generally true? Does it embrace a great amount of truth? The teachings of Christ have been perverted, and made to sanction almost every evil. Besides, a great many professing Christians have no rooted fixed abiding faith in a future life, and scarcely a belief in God, yet Theosophy teaches that—
Through all nature there is wisdom, There is goodness we may bless; In the infinite sternal We may look for happiness.

And the creatures just existing, When the change of death is o'cr, In some other form returning Taste of conscious tile once more. These ideas are, I know, ridiculed by those who pride themselves on practical wisdom, who think themselves too wise to be deceived, and perhaps have little sympathy with the deepest and noblest aspirations of mankind, or realise how infinitely little of the universe we know, but I trust that those who have leisure, and learning, and science will be careful 'o treat the ideas of Theosophy with unprejudiced consideration and justice.
Too short on earth is our uncertain stay To cast the truth in scornful pride away. Or lose the opportunity to bless And aid the cause of human happiness. Yours, &c., S. KENYON

Sir,—May I beg through you, for help for the Parochial Mission Women Association, started 30 years ago to help the poorer classes to help themselves? div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.
BY. AN EAR.LESTOViN CORRESPOEDEN T.

I notice- that several men were arraigned at New- ton the other Sattirday.on the charge of gaming with cards, at Haydock,, but as it was proved they.were orly reading " The Sunday Chronicle " they were let off. The Haydc,ck police are evidently a smart body of men, and wish they would transfer some of their smartness over to Newton. Every Sunday afternoon, almost without exception, a gang of young fellows, who would be better employed at a Sunday school, assemble in one of the Mesues fields, and for an hour or two indulge in a game of cards. Certainly they are awAy from the public thorough- fare, but if it is wrong to gamble in one place, kis equally wrong to gamble in another, and as young children wander from the footpath, in order to see what is the cause of the gathering, I think the police should take steps,to remove the devotws of the card, to some still more isolated place.

So Mr. Tom Stone, the enthusiastic Conservative athlete, who three year ,swo resided at Newton Park, has lost his vote, but the wonder is why he has been retained on the register so long. Evidently there has been a general awakening in the Liberal camp,whleh has resulted in the ,curtain being lifted from many things which haste of late been kept closely hidden. It was rather a Jong stretch to put in a claim for a vote as joint occupier of premises, that he has not seen for three yeara,and when there was much uncertainty as to when be will again take up his residence in our midst. However the matter had gone, I think it very unlikely that Mr. Stone would have travelled from Canada to record his vote for the Newton Parliamentary Divis!on.

Another interesting case which cropped up at the Recision Court was that of a blind man whose wife during the last 15 months has been in receipt of parish relief. The man seemed to feel very keenly the humiliation of having to lose his privilege of voting simply because his wife thought fit to run counter to his wishes and taccept parish assistance. The barrister of course clearly defined the law on the subject, and came to a commonsense decision on the point, by observing that if the man's wife received the relief, he must have had some benefit from the money, because it would be used for the benefit of the household. This the man could not gainsay, and he had to retire consoled by the know- ledge that he would get his vote next year, seeing that wift had ceased to receive relief.

The incident, which those who were present at the Baptist Chapel, on Monday night, witnessed was a most regrettable one, and was one which will not tend to raise the standard of religion, in the minds of those who are ever ready to pick holes in the cause. If the Baptists will invite ministers of other persuasions to take part in their social gatherings, they must carefully refrain from tread- ing upon their toes. Some men are possessed of remarkably fine susceptibilities, and Mr. Collins, an able man withal, appears to belong to this category. Re took a very wise course, however, in taking the stand be did, and I am very much inclined to think 'cid he would have been sadly blamed had he remained ,Dassire, ,undu t!)t weeping assertion that " BaptiOn 17 immersion, had been absolutely settled as the right tt,ing." The meeting was? mixed one, and the rev, gentleman from Liverpool, showed a sad want of tact, in giving utterance to his views in such an assembly.
SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE DISTRICT.

JUVENILE TEMPLARS' QUARTERLY MEETING. The Quarterly Session ot the District Juvenile Council was held in the " Raffles Memorial" Rooms, Liverpool, on Saturday, when Bro. F. W. Hall, D.S.J.T., presided over a fair attendance of repre- sentatives and visitors from temples in Liverpool, St. Helens, Warrington, Earlestown, &c. The Ses- sion opened about 4 p m., after which the usual re- ports of officers were received, these being generally of an interesting character, showing general activity in the prosecution of juvenile. templar principles—the pledge being fourfold,embracing abstinence from intoxi- cating drinks,tobacco, gambling, and profanity. A new temple had been instituted at Edge Hill, and preparations were in hand for an opening at Bootle. Activity also prevailed in the area of No. 1 Convention in our district, and there were prospects of new temples being estab- lished at Wigan, Sankey Bridges, Widnes and other places. The total membership reported was over 3,500 juveniles, with about 250 adults. Bro. IL J. White, D.C. Sec., -reported the quarter's work by the Executive Committee, and referred to the projected demonstrations in Liverpool, Southport, Sze., to celebrate the 19th anniversary of the introduc- tion of juvenile templary into England, Montpelier Temple No. 1, having been instituted at Southport on Nov. Ist., 1872. It was decided to hold the next session of the council at Earlestown during the month of Novem- ber. Reference was made to the departure from the district of Bro. J. B. Collings, G. Sec., who had been transferred to Birmingham to take charge of the Grand Lodge publishing and trading business. Several other items of business were transacted when the council ad- journed at 6 p.m. for tea. At 7 p.m., a conference was held, the attendance being increased, when interesting and instructive "papers" were read, Bro. A. Newell, P.D.S J.T., dealing with" A Model Superintendent," followed by an outline address, to a juvenile temple,after which Bro.F. W. Hall, D.S.J.T., read a paper on "Our Winter's Work."—A general dis- cussion followed the reading of the papers," the thanks of the members being accorded to the essayist, tcc.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

SERVICE OF SONG AT TFIELWALL. At the Ship Canal Mission Hall, Thelwall, on Monday, a service of song. entitled "Primrose Garth," was given. There was a full band and chorus, but in consequence of the stormy weather, there was only a moderate attend- ance, and it has been decided to repeat the performance. It is also proposed to start evening classes, which will be free later en.

div.head: ACCIDENT ON THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: ACCIDENT ON THE SHIP CANAL.

While two navvies, named Clayton and Doran, were the other morning on a" staging" suspended from one of the bridges at Latchford, the chains snapped, and precipitated them about 30 feet. It was found that Clayton had fractured one leg, and also injured his arm, while Doran had dislocated his ankle, and also had a wound in his foot. They were removed to the hospital at Latchford, where they are progressing as favourably as can be expected.

div.head: INCE SECTION.
div.p: THE INCE SECTION.

At Ellesmere Port on Tuesday night there was water to the depth of nineteen feet in the second section of the canal, and that the full depth of twenty-six feet was expected to be obtained by the end of the week. The work of filling the six miles of cutting has proceeded without mishap, under the supervision of Mr. Clarke, chief engineer, and Mr. Jones, the agent. The 29th inst. has been fixed as the date for the formal opening of through traffic on No. 1 and No. 2 sections. The dred- gers were busily engaged on Tuesday putting the finish- ing touches to the channel. No. 3 section will not be opened for several months. The gale did some slight damage to the embankments of No. 1 section, but the work of restoration has been quickly effected by Mr. Manisty, the engineer in charge. The banks are holding out splendidly. A huge steam navvy and the dredger Leven have been at work to remove the strip of land at Ellesmere Port forming the dam between the Eastham and Ince sections. The dam will eventually be removed sufficiently to allow the waters to meet, and the dredger will then be set to work to clear the whole course of the canal to the mouth of the Weaver. The dam at the mouth of the river Weaver having also been cut away, direct communication will be obtained with this river, and the traffic diverted along the Ship Canal instead of waiting for the Mersey tides.
The barque Fiji, from Liverpool to Melbourne has been wrecked on the Victorian Coast. Twelve of the crew were drowned. .

THE SECOND WARRINGTON STAR BOWEETT BUILDING SOCIETY.

' The third annual meeting of this society was held in the Legh-st. schoolroom. on Wednesday evening. Mr. John Gandy presided, and the direc- tors present were Messrs. E. Aukland, J. Hayes, W. Winstanley, J. Haywood, and G. Clay. Mr. R. Dob- son, solicitor, Messrs. J. Harrison, and E. Reddish, auditors, and Messrs Titchett,secretaries, were also present. The directors submitted their annual report as follows :—The receipts for the year are as follows :—Members' subscriptions, £1,557 17s. ; re- payment of appropriations, £273 14s. 2d.: entrance fees, fines,bank interest,transfers, &c.,£46 10s. 1d; total, .21,878 10s. 3lid. The total amount advanced is £4,270, of which there is owing £3,844 4-. 10d. The directors are pleased to report that no members are in arrears with their repayments. It is particu- larly requested that members will compare their pass books with the amounts placed to their credit and, if any discrepancy be observed, communi- cate with the secretaries immediately. Ye jollie game wych alle Creaycion lyckes, It y's ye playe of kickynge att Foote-balle ; And hym that playeth yt atween ye stycks Certs he y's ye chiefest of them alle : His head y's lyke unto a stonie walle, Ande mightie boots bath he whearwyth to lame; Full manie a foeman doth he roughlie maul, Yett Foot-balle y's a veriehollie game. Ande hym thatt playeth bac ke, wyth weightie kycks ; Ando heavie charges, tIA ait vilge foemen falle, Untyll'e ye watcher layeth tenn toe syx That he Wyll cause ye left-wynge pair for sprawl, Ande eftsoones doth he make them toe look " mane Bie heartylie projectynge ov hys frame Upon ye twayn, so they can scarcelie crawl, Yett Foote-balle ys a verie jollie game. Alsoe ye forward, wyth an hondrede trycks, (0, when he drybleth look out for a squall l) He cometh doun lyke toe a ton of brycks, Althoe he seemeth soe exceedynge small; Ande thoe hys foemen be uncommon Utile, He kycketh att their shins wyth certayne aim, (" Takynge ye mann," methynks they doe yt ca lie), Yett Foote-balle ys a verie jollie game, ENVOI&

Friends who delyte for idllie brag ande brawl, Ye who avowe thatt Tennys is toe tame, Ande lykewyse say thatt crickett lycks them all, Yet Foote-ball ys a verie jollie game. Aw've another little ditty on this gentle pastime, but awl' save id a month or two, till accidents begin; then id'll be moore appropriate nor neaw.

Aw've med up mi mind nod to let mi owdst lad be a bishop, or an archbishop! Yo know its welly eight year owd neaw, is th' child, an' its geddin' time id were doin' a bit o' summat for id keep.' Weyvin's just abeawt played eawt, an' clerkin' an skoo'-maysterin' are no better ; aw'd set mi mind on th' bishop biznes i' preference to th' inshurance line, but aw corn'd affoord th' fees, iv th' retorn printed i' some o' Wensda's popper's is correct. The Bishop o' Manchester geet off bi' payin' a trifle o'er two hundred an' seventy peawnd, but id cost Lincoln an' Peterborough moore no four hundred,an' Winchester three s's o' in a row. There isn'd mich moore werk to do th' bishop bizness nor i' th' inshurance, but there's herdly. as mich pay for Id; aw were willin' to look o'er this, though, for th' sake o' di' lad bein' co'd "mi lord," an' His Grace Turn o' Dick O'Bobs, junior. Iv th' country could go on mekkin' bishops, an' ged weel paid for doin' it, we should soon hey tuppence moore ore off tay, an' a bit off 'bacca. Onyway, aw'll th' idea to mi friend Goschen, an' he con mek wed he likes on't. I'th' meantime mi owds't lad is bent' eddicated for th' inshurance, an mi' hooaps are bias—at leeast blighted for th' present; happen when he's hed a twelvemonth at id he'll be able to pay his own fees: in fact aw'm sure he will.
