div.head: HUYTON.
div.p: HUYTON.

DROWNED 'WHILE BATIIING.—An inquest WAS held before Mr. arighouse, coroner, at the Carr's Elute!, Whis- ton, on Tuesday, touching the death of William Arthur James, 16 yea.rc of age, son of Richard James, collier, in Green's-row, who was drowned in a pit of water near fluyton Quarry ironworks on Saturday night. The evidence showed that deceased was bathing in the pit, which is about eight feet deep, and that he suddenly cried out for hrltL Several boys went to his assistance, and one named Itol)arts was grasped by the drowning youth. Roberts struggled to get away, but in vain, and he had almost succumbed when some men appeared on the scene, and he was rescued much exhausted. The body of James was recovered shortly afterwards, but life was extinct.—A verdict of "Accidentally drowned" was returned.

CARBOLIC ACID POISONING.—An inquest was held on Tuesday before Mr. S. Brighouse. coroner, at Carr's Hotel, Whiston, on the body of Thomas Roscoe, aged lb months, son of James Rosc,oe,a collier,of Carr's-cottages, who died from the effelts of carbolic acid poisoning on Sunday morning. It appeared that Mr. Rosc,oe had had several of his cilildren down with typhoid fever, and a bottle of carbolic acid was kept In one of the rooms for disinfecting t;urposes. On Monday week the deceased boy found the bottle, and before he could he stopped drank a quantity of its contents. He was attended to by Dr. Barlow, of Prescot, but expired on Sunday. It was also stated by the father that five of his children suffered from scarlet fever at one time last Christmas. The Coroner said the father had had his share of this world's troubles. A verdict of "Death by misadven- ture was returned.

div.head: FRODSTIAM.
div.p: FRODSTIAM.

HARVEST SERVICES AT PRESTON' BROOK.—On Sunday, notwithstanding the unpropitious weather, large congre- gations assembled in the Primitive Methodist Cbapel, Preston-o'-th-Hill, to hear the Rev. H. Davenport preach the sermons in connection with the harvest thanksgiving services. On Monday evening a well Attended meeting was held with the same object, wheo addresses were der livered by the Revs. Martin an Finch, of Runcorn, and H. Davenport. Anthems were sung bf tio choir. The chapel was tastefully decorated. MUSICAL ESTERTAINMENT.-011Sday &Veiling, a concert was given in the Town Hall, Frodsham, by the choir of the Princess Alice Orphanage, Birmingham, numbering some 20 voices. The hall was tilled to ex- cess iay an appreciative audience. The items on the programme were of an interesting character, and were much enjoyed, and consisted of many choice solos, an- thems, choruses,and action songs. During the interval, Mr. Durley, governor of the Orphanage, gave a descrip- tion of the objects in view, and other information respecting the Children's Horne. Miss Fanny Tye ac- companied throughout very effectively. METHODIST FREE CHURCH.—Harvest thanksgivinc, ser- vices were held on Sunday in the above church, and ;in harmony with the prevailing custom, the interior of the building had been tastefully decoratod with ccrn, choice fruits, flowers, and vegetables. Appropriate sermons were preached by the :Rev. R. Trotter' in the afternoon and evening, to large congregations. On Monday even- ing a public meeting was held, which was presided over by Mr. James Brandreth, of Helsby, when addresses were given by the Rev. R. Trotter and several members of the congregation. The usual vote of thanks to the Chairman closed a very pleasant meeting. FRODSHAII BRIDGE MILLS.—On Saturday the whole of ' the employes engaged by Messrs. Thomas Rigby and Sons, with their wives had their first annual excursion. The party left Sutton Bridge by the mill steamer Peter at 4.30 a.m for Liverpool, arriving at the Alexander Dock at 7.30. After partaking of a substantial break- fast, which had been provided at the Aiexandra Dock branch of the British Workman Public-house Company, an inspection was mad() (by those who desired) of the I grain storage warehouses, and the party then took the 'bus atom=" the line of docks to the landing-stage, where they took boat for New Brighton. Dinner was also pro- vided here for the party at 12.30. After spending several hours, making the most of the attractions which New Brighton is noted for, the party returned to Liverpool, the Peter being in readiness to return, and the sail home- wards was much enjoved,Sutton Bridge being reached about 6 p.m. The whole of the expenses were defrayed by Messrs. Rigby, and as this, the first trip, was one of such a happy character, the party look forward to a similar next year.

div.head: LONGFORD WIFE MURDER.
div.p: THE LONGFORD WIFE MURDER.

At Longford. on Thursday, James Heany and his father,Thomas Heany, were committed for trial, charged with the murder of Mary Ann Heany, wife of the first named prisoner. Thu evidence was to the effect that during the quarrel in a field the prisoners attacked the woman, and that James Heany fatally wounded her with a scythe.

div.head: GENERAL BOOTH AT MELBOURNE.
div.p: GENERAL BOOTH AT MELBOURNE.

Tuesday, General Booth's last day in Melbourne, was devoted to a public explanation of the social regenera- tion schema. In the afternoon he lectured in the Athemeum before 1,000 persons. Sir M. H. Davies, Speaker of the Legislative Assembly, presided, and Sir James Macbain, president of the Legislative Council,and a number of members of Parliament and leading clergy- men were present. The lecture met with a hearty recep- tion. Immense enthusiasm was displayed by the 10,000 persons whom the General addressed in the evening.
EXTRAORDINARY SHOOTING FATALITY.

A shocking fatality occurred on Wednesday morning on the shore near St. Michael's. Sergeant William Montague, of the Liverpool constabulary, was shooting on the shore, along with a pork butcher named James Hodgson and a ship's quartermaster named Edwin Johns, when the gun carried by Sergeant Montague accidentally went off, tke contents lodging in the fore- head of Johns and killing him on the spot. An addi- tionally sad feature of the affair is that the widow is left with six children totally unprovided for.

div.head: ADVENTURE OF A YOUNG LADY.
div.p: ADVENTURE OF A YOUNG LADY.

A young lady named Yeatman, of Enfield, Middlesex, who has been spending the summer at Scove, near Ilfracombe, on Wednesday experienced an extraordinary adventure. In the afternoon she left home to bathe, and did not return. Fruitless search was made by her mother and friends during the evening and early on Thursday morning, about ten o'clock, two sailors row- ing round the coast found the young lady standing in the water at the bottom of a creek, and rescued her. She had occupied her precarious position 13 hours. She was wandering in her mind, and was unable to account for herself, but it is surmised that she slipped from the cliffs. Her head and legs were severely cut. She is recovering under medical supervision.

div.head: CHEMICAL WORKS FATALITY AT
div.p: THE CHEMICAL WORKS FATALITY AT
ST. HELENS.

On Saturday afternoon, Mr. S. Brighouse. county coroner, held an inquest at the Town Hall, touching the death of William Beswick, 27 years of age, of 23 Langtree-street, St. Helens, who was killed by the collapse of a portion of the old St. Helens Chemical Works, on Thursday afternoon. William Penketh Beswick, of 44, Peel House-lane, Widnes, deposed that the deceased was his son.—William Penning- ton, 23, Langtree-street, St. Helens, said he was foreman of the men engaged pulling down the old St. Helens Chemical Works, and they were all employed by Mr. John Burton, contractor, Widnes. On Thursday they were taking down the timbers and supports of the department known as Weldon's plant. The pans were removed some four or five weeks ago, but the last portion was taken off the timbers on the morning of the acci- dent, leaving nothing but the framework. None of the bolts or screws of the framework had been touched. The framework was about 30ft. in length, 14ft. wide, and 37ft. in height. When the pans were removed the frame- work did not move or vibrate to the slightest extent. The deceased man Beswick was on the top of the frame- work, and the man James Gaffney, who was badly in- jured, sat on a beam abut 10ft. below. There was not the least indication that the structure was unsafe, and witness himself wag on the top about two minutes before it collapsed. The framework fell over sideways, and Bcswick died in about two minutes after being picked up.—James Caunce, a workman, gave similar evidence. Some of the jurors expressed the opinion that the removal of the pans would cause the timber to spring upwards and make the framework top-heavy.—Another juryman said he had examined the timber, and portions of it ap- peared to have been eaten away by acid from the pans.— The witness Pennington, on being re-called, said that the structure was inspected in the morning,and so far as out- ward indications went it was perfectly safe and sound.— Mr. John Burton, contractor, gave evidence that the structure was being taken down in the safest way, and that there were no indications of danger. He was dues- tionsd as to the advisability of strengthening the timbers by chains or stays, and he said it was not considered necessary under the circumstances. If there had been any signs of danger he should have done it.—The Coroner, in summing up, remarked that it was for the jury to say whether or not they considered all reasonable precautions had been taken for the safety of the men.—The jury re- turned a verdict of "Accidental death," adding that they thought more precautions might have been taken by staying the timber before taking off the top pieces.

div.head: SHOCKING FATALITY AT HAYDOCK.
div.p: SHOCKING FATALITY AT HAYDOCK.

About half-past two on Wednesday morning, an old man named Moses Hayes, 66 years of age, residing at 9, Warrington-road, Ashton, met with his death in a shock- ing manner, while following his employment as day wageman in No 3, old Boston pit, Haydock. The deceased was a collier, named John Cullen, and was engaged taking a prop from under the main arch of old Boston pit. Mr. W. Pilling, the foreman called Cullen away, and on returning the latter found that the first ring of the arching had given way, and almost buried Hayes beneath the debris. Cullen ran for assistance, and Haves was extricated, and removed to the top of the shaft, and conveyed home, but he died soon after arrival.

div.head: DEAF AND DUMB MAN DRUNK.
div.p: A DEAF AND DUMB MAN DRUNK.

Before Messrs. T. J. Gillespie and T. D. Grimke- Drayton. at the Town Hall, Newton, on Monday, John Pickavance, a deaf and dumb man, belong- ing to St. llo,lens, was brought up .charged with be- ing drunk in Earlestown on Saturday night, and fined ss. and casts, and in default was sent to gaol for 14 days. NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS MUSICAL SOCIETY.

The annual —general meeting of the members of this society was held in the Congregational School- room, Newton, on Tuesday night. Mr. F. J. Holmes presided, and there was a good attendance. The financial statement for the past session was sub- mitted by Mr. C. B. Corlett, and accepted as satisfactory, the balance of 4s. being carded forward to the ensuing session. The election of officers' was then proceeded with, Mr. F. J. Holmes being elected vice-president, Mr. C. B. Corlett, secretary, Mr. E. Corlett, conductor, and Mr. W. Thompson, pianist. The following were chosen as the Committee, Messrs. R. Owen, J. W. Glover, W. Thompson. C. Pritchard, Pryon, Duncalf. Latchford, W. Welsh, J. Nichols and G. Kidd. It is in contem- plation to bring out Cowen's cantata "Rose Maiden," and preparations for its production will commence on Monday night.

ATTEMPTFD MURDER ON A WELSH MOUNTAIN. Mr. Day.led Teged Jones, farmer, Gonna. Traws- fynydd, Merionethshire, was found ou Thursday on the mountain side in an unconscious condition and terribly battered about the head and body. There were indications all round of a desperate struggle with his assailants, who we not known. Mr. Jones was carried to his house, where he lies in a critical condition.

div.head: SHOCKING' RAILWAY ACCIDENTS.
div.p: SHOCKING' RAILWAY ACCIDENTS.

Two serious accidents occurred at Crewe yesterday morning. A pointsman named Richard Cheaters was walking down the line to his box, when in stepping out of the way of one train he was knocked down by another and terribly injured.—The other victim was James Wood- row, porter, who attempting to jump on a moving train, slipped and was dragged between the carriages and platform, one leg being torn off.

div.head: LIVERPOOL THEATRE BURNT DOWN.
div.p: A LIVERPOOL THEATRE BURNT DOWN.

The Gaiety Theatre of Varieties, Camden-st., Liver- pool, was destroyed by fire yesterday morning, and the bare walls and iron columns only are now left standing. The first alarm was given to the fire brigade about eight, and by the time the engines arrived the flames were shooting up to a great height through the roof, and it was not found possible to save the building from des- truction. The origin of the fire is not known.

A SCHoOLMASTER AND ORGANIST COMMITTED. At Denbigh, yesterday, J. W. Barnwell, schoolmaster and church organist at Llandyrnog, was committed for trial charged with haying unlawfully assaulted his niece, Rose Allen, of Reading, whom he had adopted as his child, and who is now twelve years and eleven months old. Medical evidence v. as given. The girl was expect- ing shortly to be confined, and it was stated that the prisoner had admitted his guilt to the girl's father.

div.head: QUEEN OF ROUMANIA.
div.p: THE QUEEN OF ROUMANIA.
_ PALLANZA, FRIDAY.—The health of the Queen of Roumania is improving slightly. She is able to stand and walk about for a few minutes every day.
MASSACRE OF WHITES BY INDIANS.

NEW Ironic, FRIDAY.—It is reported that a party of whites has 'wen slaughtered by Indians in Alaska. It is believed that amongst the victims is an Englishman named Herbert Earlscliffe. THE ST. MAUDE DISASTER.

PARIS, FRIDAY AFTEROON.—Caron, the engine-driver, and Deguerrois, the deputy station-mastor, have been found guilty of culpable negligence which led to the dis- astrous railway collision at St. Maude. Caron was sen- tenced to two years' imprisonment, and Deguerrois to four months. EXPLOSION IN AMERICA. FOUR LIVES LOST. •

NEWARK (NEW JERSNY), FRlDAY.—During the celebra- bration here yesterday by a number of Italians of the Feast of San Rocca a mortar prematurely exploded. Four of the Italians were killed on the spot, while 30 others were more or less seriously injured. THE SPANISH RAILWAY ACCIDENT.

The Press Association is informed that the telegram which Mrs. Seymour Lucas received on Thursday in reference to a railway accident in Spain, came from Burgos. It was stated that her husband was injnred, but not dangorotisly. -Since Mrs. Lucas left for Burgos a telegram has been received at her residence stating that Mr. Maurice Long was among the killed. MADRID, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—In addition to those whose names have been already teleg,raphed, it has been asctertained that Mr. Fletcher, son of Professor Banister Fletcher, of London, was injured in the railway accident near Burgos. Most of the injured are making satisfac- tory progress. An official inquiry as to the responsi- bility of the disaster has been ordered. The total num- ber of lives lost is 24.
SIX MEN COMMITTED FOR MURDER.

At Kanturk on Thursday, Major Hutchinson, R.M., committed for trial six men, named David Delury, Timothy Harrington, Denis Brien, Patrick Murphy, Jere- miah Mahony, and Michael Power, for the wilful murder of Patrick Connell, who was waylaid and killed near Kanturk a few weeks ago.
THE BLNCKPOOL EIFFEL TOWER.

Blackpool was en fete yesterday on the occasion of the laying of the foundation-stone of the Eiffel Tower by Sir Matthew White Ridley, member for the Blackpool Parliamentary Division. The Mayors of about thirty Lancashire, Yorkshire and Midland boroughs were present, and special trains brought crowds of visitors to the town. The stone laying ceremony was preceded by a procession, including Vie lifeboat and fire brigades, the volun- teers, several bands, km. A banquet followed and there were fireworks from both piers at nights.

div.head: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.
KIRKDALE.

Last evening at Lambeth Hall, the Executive Committee of the Kirkdale Labour Electoral Asso- ciation presented Mr. T.R. Thelfall, Southport, with a requisition from the electors of Kirkdale inviting him to contest the Parliamentary division. WEST BRADFORD.

A telegram was received in Bradford on Thursday from Mr. Ben Tillett, announcing that the Dockers' Union had consented to his becoming a labour can- didate for the Western Division of Bradford. He had been previously asked to stand for the division but withheld his decision until he had consulted' the union. The present member for the division is Mr. Illingworth, who was elected by a majority of 1,352 in 1886, his opponent then being Mr. Virling, Liberal Unionist.
MR. GLADSTONE'S JOURNEY TO

div.head: SCOTLAND.
div.p: SCOTLAND.

Mr. Gladstone, accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone and Mr. and Mrs. Henry Gledstone, left llawarden Castle on Thursday night for Fasque, Kincardine- shire, the seat of Sir John Gladstone, on a visit for a few days, after which he will proceed to New- castle-on-Tyne for the annual meeting of the National Liberal Federation. Mr. and Mrs. Glad- stone drove from the Castle at 9.30 to Broughton Hall Station, on the Chester, Mold, and Denbigh Railway, where a saloon carriage was in readiness attached to a special train, which left for Chester at 10.15, where there was a brief stay for the Scotch express from Euston due out from Crewe at 11.29 The stoppages on the journey were Wigan (12.20) and Carlisle (2.30). Mr. Gladstone has quite thrown off the after-effects of the influenza, and he will probably be able to fulfil his engagement at New- castle-on-Tyne without any unpleasant consequ- ences to his health. There were only a few people on the platform at Chester as the express entered the station. There was no demonstration, the right honourable gentleman having expressed a desire to pass through quietly.
Reports from Ostend tend to confirm the rumour that Mr. Stanley has resigned the Governorship of the Congo State, and that the post has been offered to a German officer now serving in Algeria. .

COLLISION ON THE MERSEY. _- A disastrous collision occurred, early on Wednesday morning, off the mouth of the Mersey, the. Glasgow steamer Lugar being sunk by the steamer Saxon Prince, from Huelva to Garston. The Lugar went down so sud- denly that the crew escaped with the utmost difficulty. They were safely landed by the steamer Kildare. The Saxon Prince had previously been in collision with the Harrison liner Mira, which vessel has been docked for repairs.
